en: The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Bhadrapāla-parivarta, Scroll One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty. Chapter One:
The Chapter on Contemplation. Chapter One: The Chapter on Contemplation.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—their outflows exhausted, free from further afflictions, and having attained mastery;
their minds well-liberated and their wisdom well-liberated, they were as thoroughly tamed as great elephants.
Having accomplished what was to be done and perfected all practices, they have laid down the heavy burden and will not undergo further rebirth;
practicing equanimity, they have attained their own true benefit, dwelling securely in the True Teaching and reaching the further shore—with the sole exception of the Elder Ānanda.

At that time, there were also five hundred bhikṣus who, at the hour of dawn, each departed from their respective dwellings and went to where the World-Honored One was. With palms joined in reverence, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having completed their summer retreat in Śrāvastī, traveled by stages through cities and villages together with five hundred bhikṣus until they reached Rājagṛha. They entered the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery and approached the place where the World-Honored One was staying.
Having arrived, they paid homage by prostrating at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, through his supernormal powers, radiated a great majestic light, causing all the bhikṣus residing in every kingdom, city, town, and village to come together to the great city of Rājagṛha. They entered the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery and approached the place where the World-Honored One was; there, with palms joined in reverence, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus from the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery, moved by the Buddha’s majestic radiance, had all gathered like clouds at the World-Honored One’s dwelling. With palms joined in reverence, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there was also the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī—likewise sustained by the World-Honored One’s majestic spiritual power—who, together with twenty thousand bhikṣuṇīs, all assembled in great numbers, entered the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery and approached the place where the World-Honored One was. With palms joined in reverence, she prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there was an upāsaka named Bhadrapāla, who was the leader of the assembly. He was accompanied by five hundred other upāsakas—all of whom observed the five precepts and were perfect in their dignified conduct. These were great bodhisattvas who had long since established themselves in the practice of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

By the power of their original vows, they constantly followed the World-Honored One and delighted in hearing the True Dharma; they were ever diligent and persevering in order to fulfill all the dharmas that assist the Path.

At dawn, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they departed from their respective residences and entered the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery to reach the presence of the World-Honored One. With palms joined in reverence, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.

At that time, in the great city of Vaiśālī, there was a Licchavi named Ratnasaṃbhava, who was the leader of the assembly. Together with twenty-eight thousand other Licchavis, he set out from that city at dawn, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, and arrived at this Kalandakanivāpa grove where the Tathāgata was staying. With palms joined in reverence, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there was a son of an elder in the city of Campā named Tārakopaga, who was the leader of a great multitude. Together with twenty-eight thousand sons of elders, he set out from the city of Campā at dawn, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, and arrived at this Kalandakanivāpa grove where the World-Honored One was staying. There, he joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there was also a māṇava—translated in the Sui language as "Pure Holder," or alternatively "Youth," or "Benevolent Boy"—named Naladatta, who served as the leader of the assembly. Together with twenty-eight thousand people, he set out from his own residence at dawn and entered this Karanda Garden to approach the World-Honored One. With palms joined in reverence, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there was also in the kingdom of Śrāvastī an elder named Mahāsārthavāha, together with the elder Anāthapiṇḍada, who served as leaders of the assembly; accompanied by twenty-eight thousand people, they departed from Śrāvastī for Rājagṛha, entering the Kalandakanivāpa grove to the place where the World-Honored One was. With reverence and palms joined, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there was another elder named Varuṇa, who was the foremost among them; accompanied by twenty-eight thousand people, he set out from his original residence and entered this Kalandakanivāpa grove to approach the World-Honored One. With palms joined in reverence, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī, together with hundreds of thousands of his retinue, also arrived at this Kalandakanivāpa grove at the hour of dawn to approach the World-Honored One. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, furthermore, the Four Great Heavenly Kings and Śakra, Lord of Devas, as well as all the celestial hosts of the desire realm, each accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of attendant celestial beings, also arrived at the Kalandaka Garden at dawn and approached the Tathāgata. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there was also Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, accompanied by an assembly of countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of celestial followers. In the early morning, they all entered the Kalandaka Garden and approached the place where the Tathāgata was; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the Great Lord Mahesvara King, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of deities from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, also entered the Kalandaka Grove at dawn; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there were also four asura kings, each accompanied by an immeasurable hundred-thousandfold retinue of asuras, who likewise entered the Kalandaka Grove at dawn and approached the place where the Tathāgata was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there were also the Nanda Dragon King and the Upananda Dragon King, each accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dragon followers, who likewise entered the Kalandaka Garden at dawn to approach the Tathāgata. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, there were also the Naga King Sagara, the Naga King Anavatapta, as well as the Naga King Manasvin and the Naga King Elapatra, each accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of naga followers. They too entered the Kalandaka Grove at dawn, approached the Tathāgata’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, all the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās of this trichiliocosm, as well as all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and even humans and non-humans, along with the kings and others who had faith in the Tathāgata, gathered at the Kalandakanivāpa Grove to go to the place where the Tathāgata was for the sake of hearing the Dharma. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and each sat to one side.

At that time, the grounds of the Kalandaka Grove were so vast and expansive that the entire area of the trichiliocosm was filled with the great assembly, leaving no vacant space even as small as the tip of a staff that was not pervaded by them.

Thus, from the Peak of Existence above down to the Brahma palaces below, all the great assemblies of devas possessing majestic power and supernormal faculties, as well as all the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth, all came to assemble.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the doubts in my mind; I wonder, World-Honored One, will you deign to listen?
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying:
“Bhadrapāla! Whatever you may doubt, ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you so as to bring you joy.”
At that time, having received permission, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By accomplishing which samādhi does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become endowed with and able to attain that great mass of merit?”
How does one enter the great ocean of extensive learning and obtain the treasury of wisdom, so as to have no doubts when questioned?
Furthermore, how does one attain the aggregate of mental discipline (*manas-saṃvara-skandha*) without loss or failure, so as to never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Furthermore, how can one avoid falling into ignorance and false views regarding the state of emptiness?
How can one attain the knowledge of past lives in order to fully comprehend the past and the future?
And how can one ensure that one never ceases to behold the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and hear the True Dharma, even in dreams?
How shall one obtain an exceptionally distinguished, upright, and sublime physical form, endowed with perfect deportment, so that all sentient beings delight in beholding it?
How shall one always be born into a family of great lineage and a position of honor, so that all who see one pay them respect?
How, furthermore, can one obtain parents, brothers, kinsmen, retinues, and spiritual friends to surround them on all sides, so that they are never separated?
How should one attain broad mastery and extensive erudition, such that one's deeds are extraordinary and never deficient, because of the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
How should one attain right mindfulness and right conduct, remaining steadfast in their discipline and content in mind?
How should one always give rise to shame and remorse, thereby remaining far removed from disgrace?
How should one attain right wisdom and humility in order to subdue the conceit of "I"?
How should one attain diligent exertion in order to remain far removed from indolence?
How shall one attain great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, so as to bestow happiness upon all with impartiality?
How shall one attain such a state that when hearing the teaching of the profound, empty, signless, and wishless Dharma, there is no fear or despondency whatsoever?
How shall one attain freedom from the indolence of non-delight by means of upholding the True Dharma?
How shall one attain wisdom that penetrates all things, clearly understanding that there is none equal to it?
How should one act so as to be able to take birth at will in all Buddha-fields?
How should one act so as not to be defeated or destroyed by any non-Buddhist paths?
How should one attain being like the ocean, so as to be able to receive and contain all questions and doubts, resolving difficulties without diminution or exhaustion?
How should one attain being like the full moon, so as to be complete in all pure and white dharmas?
How should one attain that which is like the rising sun, because it shatters all darkness?
How should one attain that which is like a lamp or torch, because its radiance illuminates with clarity?
How should one attain that which is like the nature of space, because it is free from all obstruction?
How should one attain non-abiding and non-attachment, so that the mind is like empty space?
How should one attain the nature of a vajra, so as to pierce through and penetrate all phenomena?
How should one attain being like Mount Sumeru, because of being unshakable?
How should one attain being like a door-sill, because of abiding correctly in all things?
How should one attain being like cats, dogs, and other animals, because of the accomplishment of mental karma?
How shall one attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within all phenomena?
How shall one attain the ability to go wherever one wishes, like a bird in flight?
How shall one attain the crushing of pride, like the son of a *caṇḍāla*?

How should one dwell in an araṇya so that, like wild beasts, monkeys, and the like, one takes no delight in cities or villages, and so that all those who have gone forth and those who remain at home do not become entangled with one another?
How shall one come to preside over the great assembly, so as to instruct, admonish, and guide them?
How shall one come to take no pleasure in being born among any sentient beings, yet remain unmoved by all sentient beings?
How shall one attain such a state as not to be overcome by any heterodox teachers or to be confused by celestial Māras?
How shall one attain great eloquence, through the definitive understanding and realization of all phenomena?
How shall one attain [mastery] over all Buddha-dharmas so as not to follow the lead of others?
How shall one attain great, firm faith that is indestructible?
How shall one obtain the power of great compassion, so that faith is unshakable?
How shall one obtain deep entry into faith, so that there is nothing to be practiced?
How shall one obtain moistening faith, so as to experience great joy within all dharmas?
How shall one attain supreme faith, by never tiring of making offerings to and serving all Buddhas?
How shall one attain various modes of entry into faith, by planting all roots of goodness?
How shall one attain true and wondrous faith, so as to increase conduct free from hypocrisy?
How shall one attain pure and joyful faith, so as to eliminate all jealousy?
How should one attain pure faith, for the sake of obtaining the light of all-knowledge?
How should one attain the faith of joyful practice, for the sake of eliminating all hindrances and obstacles to evil?
How should one attain the faith of the joy of wisdom, by virtue of embracing the spheres of all Buddhas?
How should one attain the faith of adorned practice, by virtue of the pure accomplishment of a Buddha-land that surpasses all worldly ornaments and adornments?
How shall one attain pure conduct of the precepts, so as to forever extinguish all thoughts of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
How shall one attain the adornment of great vows, so that all that is undertaken reaches ultimate fulfillment?
How shall one become a leader among all sentient beings in order to practice all wholesome dharmas?
How shall one attain freedom from weariness in order to instruct all bodhisattvas in the various pāramitās they must study?
How should one attain non-retrogression, by seeking all Buddha-dharmas extensively?
How should one attain indestructibility, so as not to be defeated by any heterodox teachers or false masters?
How should one attain deep faith in all Buddhas, so as not to abandon this mindfulness and to see the Buddhas constantly?
How should one conceive of them as one's father, so as to perpetuate and uphold all Buddha-dharma?
How shall one obtain the empowerment of the Buddha's power so as to be born within the radiance of all Buddha-dharmas?
How shall one obtain non-obstruction so that all Buddha-dharmas manifest before one?
How should one become like an illusory person, because of having no thoughts regarding any phenomena?
How should one become like a magical creation, because of observing that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing?
How should one attain the state of being like a dream, by observing that the three periods of time have neither coming nor going?
How should one attain the state of being like a reflected image, so that all worlds manifest within one's own body?
How should one attain that which is like an echo—how, because all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, are they without action and unconditioned?
How should one attain that which is like a reflection—how, regarding all produced phenomena, is there naturally no mental grasping or rejection?
How should one attain emptiness and non-existence by remaining far removed from all conceptualizations of phenomena?
How should one attain signlessness by contemplating that all dharmas are without duality?
How shall one attain the limit of the dharma-realm, because the bodhicitta is immeasurable?
How shall one attain non-attachment, because the nature of all worlds is without discrimination?
How shall one attain unimpeded conduct, so as to travel throughout all Buddha-fields?
How shall one attain the various dhāraṇīs, such that by hearing one thing one knows ten thousand, and skillfully masters the analytical explanations of all written characters?
How shall I come to be like those Dharma masters, who skillfully know all Buddha-dharmas?
How shall I come to be protected and remembered by all Buddhas, and sustained by the majestic power of all Buddhas?
How shall one attain heroic vigor and freedom from timidity, so as to possess a voice like that of a great bull king and the stride of a great lion king?
How shall one attain fearlessness, so as to cause all the worlds to rejoice?
How shall one attain freedom from doubt, because all Buddhas are equal and non-dual?
How shall one attain penetration of suchness (*tathatā*) and eliminate doubt, by not clinging to any phenomena?
How shall one realize the profound realm of reality (dharmadhātu) so as to be well able to explain the meaning of what is asked?
How shall one become a teacher who benefits others by being fully endowed with great compassion?
How should one eliminate laziness so as to always delight in preaching the Dharma?
How should one abide in accordance with the Dharma so as not to abandon any sentient being?
How shall one attain freedom from guile and crookedness, because of having a nature that is pure and straightforward?
How shall one attain being like eyes, because of serving as a lamp of illumination for all the world?
How should one attain the state of being beyond contempt, so as to transcend all the three realms?
How should one attain freedom from contentious debate, by practicing according to the teachings?
How shall one attain freedom from hardship, by practicing without dwelling or attachment?
How shall one come to know the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), by not discriminating among phenomena?
How shall I attain the wisdom of all speech so that I may cause all sentient beings to abide in the Mahāyāna?
How shall I reach the state of fearlessness, remaining far removed from terror and forever free from such occurrences as the bristling of body hair?
How should one know that the Buddha speaks through skillful means, because he has thoroughly mastered all sūtras and so forth?
How should one attain non-empty birth in the world, constantly entering all assemblies to obtain benefit?
How shall one become the foremost of all-knowing ones, possessing great renown such that one should receive offerings from all worlds?
How shall one attain boundless praise and merit, becoming a field of blessings for all sentient beings?
How shall one attain immeasurable great joy and exultation, by virtue of always remaining beneath the lion thrones of all Tathāgatas?
How shall one attain supreme eloquence, so as to be able to inquire about all Buddha-dharmas?
How shall one attain eloquence such that the mind is not timid or weak, being free from fear in the midst of all assemblies?
How shall one attain a debating eloquence like that of a lion king, so as to subdue all non-Buddhists and to gather in all teachers of divergent doctrines?
How should one attain the adornment of unbreakable original vows, in order to destroy all factions of heterodox and deviant views?
How should one attain skillful preaching of the Dharma and always occupy the lion’s throne, being certified by the seal of approval of all Buddhas?
How shall one come to be far removed from all worldly and meaningless speech, by means of penetrating all true teachings?
How shall one come to deeply love all the Buddha-dharmas, by practicing within the birthplaces of all Tathāgatas?
How should one come to delight in the true Dharma, knowing that all Tathāgatas are unborn?
How should one come to be free from indolence and pride, through skillfully serving spiritual friends?
How should one attain non-attachment so as to travel through all worlds?
How should one attain the fulfillment of vows and practices so as to transform and guide all sentient beings?
How should one attain that which is like coral, by virtue of attaining all the marks?
How should one attain that which is like space, because all dharmas lack the mark of being attained?
How should one attain that which is like a bodhisattva, so as not to sever the lineage of the Buddhas?
How shall they attain non-ceasing [practice], so as never to be separated from the Mahāyāna while traversing the bodhisattva paths?
How shall they don the great armor, so as to dwell with certainty within the vast precepts of all Buddhas?
How shall one obtain the empowerment praised by all Buddhas and abide in the stage of the ten powers of all Tathāgatas?
How shall one attain mastery over all that is conceived and penetrate the practice of all dharmas?
How should one attain all forms of calculation through skillful means?
How should one thoroughly understand all processes of formation and destruction by remaining far removed from all obstructive practices?
How should one attain the practice of non-abiding in all things, by neither grasping nor rejecting?
How should one become a great donor of all things, capable of giving without regret?
How shall one enter the ocean of all dharmas, so as to be able to bestow the supreme treasury of the Dharma-jewels?
How shall one engage in the conduct of all worlds, so as to be able to relinquish all worldly signs?
How shall one attain vast and great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) so as to accord with the supernormal powers of all Buddhas and be fulfilled in joy?
How shall one attain the power to travel in a single kṣaṇa and reach the presence of all Buddhas everywhere?

Furthermore, how shall one come to dwell in this Buddha-field so as to see all Buddhas of the ten directions, hear the True Dharma, and make offerings to the Sangha; and while not yet having attained the six supramundane powers, nor indeed even the five mundane powers, yet without abandoning this physical body in this world and without being born in those other Buddha-lands, but rather dwelling in this very land to see the Buddhas and World-Honored Ones of other worlds, hearing the True Dharma proclaimed by all those Buddhas, receiving and upholding it all, and practicing according to what was taught?
“World-Honored One!
Just as at this very time the Venerable Ānanda, having personally heard the Dharma from the World-Honored One, receives and upholds it all and practices according to the teaching;

so too are those bodhisattvas, who, while residing in this land without traveling to that realm, are able to behold all Buddhas and World-Honored Ones, and having heard the Dharma, are able to receive and uphold it all and practice according to the teaching.”
From this time forward, in all places of birth, they shall never be separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and shall hear the True Dharma; even in their dreams, it shall always be thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Bhadrapāla!”

That you are now able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a profound and subtle meaning is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings in the world, for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, out of compassion for gods and humans, and to sustain and uphold all bodhisattvas in future ages.
“Bhadrapāla!

In the past, you have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, planted various roots of goodness, heard the true Dharma, upheld the true Dharma, delighted in the true Dharma, and revered the true Dharma.”

It is solely because you, Mahākāśyapa, practice the teachings through transformation that you possess few desires and know contentment, always delighting in secluded forest hermitages (araṇya)—whether dwelling among graves, beneath trees, or sitting in the open air; you constantly sit without lying down, remaining on a single mat without moving; you accept the practice of alms-gathering, eating once and not a second time, either eating in a single sitting or consuming only a single morsel; you maintain only the three robes and rag-robes (pāṃsukūla), praise the dhūta ascetic practices, exhort all bodhisattvas, teach the bodhisattva path, cause all bodhisattvas to rejoice, reprove all bodhisattvas, instruct all bodhisattvas, and bring all bodhisattvas to fulfillment; you are able to perform beneficial deeds of great compassion and give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.

All have attained mastery and reached the other shore; they are able to behold all Buddhas at will, giving rise to vast vows and practicing profound and wondrous deeds. They take delight in the pillar of omniscient bodhi, skillfully conforming to the lineage of the Tathāgatas, and generating a bodhicitta as indestructible as a vajra.
They thoroughly comprehend the thoughts of sentient beings in the world; their vast and wondrous conduct is beyond calculation or measure, and they are ever present before the eyes of all Buddhas.
Bhadrapāla!
Not even a small portion of your merits has been described.
"Bhadrapāla! [he said].
Now there is a bodhisattva samādhi called the "Samādhi of Contemplating All Buddhas Appearing Before One.
If a bodhisattva fully cultivates this samādhi, they shall achieve all the aforementioned merits and qualities.
"Bhadrapāla, you should know that there are further immeasurable and boundless supreme merits that cannot be fully described.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"

I only pray that you will explain this Bodhisattva Samādhi of Mindfulness of All Buddhas Standing Before One, so that the gods, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans in this world may obtain great benefit and receive much peace and happiness; and so that immeasurable sentient beings in the future may likewise obtain great benefit and receive peace and happiness; and furthermore, so that it may serve as a great illumination for future bodhisattvas and provide them with the power of reception.
Furthermore, may all bodhisattvas of the present and future universally hear this Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of All Buddhas;
having heard it, may they all receive and uphold it;
and having received and upheld it, may they all practice and train according to reality, and carry out its teachings as instructed.

Once they have studied and practiced, they shall be caused to attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and will be able to manifest and fully accomplish such merits as well as other superior and sublime virtues.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying: "Bhadrapāla!
As you have said, you should listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall now analyze and explain it for you."
Bhadrapāla spoke again:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
I deeply delight in hearing what the Tathāgata has taught.”
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Bhadrapāla! What is called the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Contemplating All Buddhas as Manifestly Present Before One?"

If there is a bodhisattva who fully accomplishes this samādhi, they will immediately obtain all the aforementioned meritorious qualities as well as other extraordinary merits, namely: all Buddhas will appear before them whenever they bring them to mind; their minds will remain undisturbed, and they will not abandon their activities.
Seeking supreme wisdom with courageous diligence, they shoulder the heavy burden of delivering sentient beings across [samsara].
They serve and provide for all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), constantly cultivating the vast contemplation of emptiness and quiescence.
Associate with virtuous spiritual friends, eliminate all hindrances, distance oneself from evil associates, cease worldly talk, and close the gates of the sense faculties.

During the first, middle, and last watches of the night, diminish sleep; do not crave clothing, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, halls, houses, couches, seats, or various requisites; always delight in solitude, dwelling in an araṇya.

One does not cherish one's own body, nor does one prize one's life; one is not attached to form or color, nor does one indulge the mind. One cultivates through a heart of loving-kindness, perfumes oneself with the practice of compassion, rejoices at all times, and constantly practices equanimity.
Destroying the afflictions and accomplishing the various dhyānas, one contemplates within them without attachment to their flavor.

Observing that the perception of form yields nothing but an empty mind, one does not disturb right mindfulness; one does not grasp at the aggregates, does not cling to the sense bases, does not contemplate the elements, and does not crave places of birth.
He subdues pride and arrogance, does not envy the wealth of others, and brings great benefit to all the world.
He gives rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, regards all sentient beings as his own parents, and maintains the thought of regarding all sentient beings as his only child.

Among all phenomena, there is no notion of contention; though one maintains the precepts through mindfulness, one does not cling to them; though one constantly dwells in meditative concentration, one is free from indulgence or attachment.

One delights in extensive learning without giving rise to discrimination; the aggregate of ethical discipline is unimpaired, the aggregate of concentration is immovable, and the aggregate of wisdom is non-delusory.
They have no doubts regarding all phenomena; they do not turn their backs on the Buddhas, do not slander the True Dharma, do not disrupt the Sangha, and do not take pleasure in discord.
They draw near to the noble ones, distance themselves from ignorance, and do not seek after worldly transcendence.
Although they hear spoken words, their minds do not delight in listening to them, nor do they become attached to the six worldly flavors.

They practice and cultivate the five dharmas of liberation, eliminate the ten unwholesome deeds, and mindfully cultivate the ten wholesome deeds. They sever the nine bases of affliction for sentient beings, and their minds never depart from the gate of the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*). They constantly contemplate abandoning the eight kinds of indolence and single-mindedly cultivate the eight awakenings of the great person (*aṣṭamahāpuruṣavibhāga*). They do not cling to the flavor of dhyāna nor rely on their extensive learning; they subdue their pride and listen with a single mind.

Seeking the Dharma with earnest gravity, practicing the path to realization, and out of compassion for sentient beings, one abandons the discrimination of self; one finds that the notion of seeking a life-span is ultimately difficult to attain, observes the aggregates as being without substantiality, and neither dwells in nirvana nor clings to saṃsāra.
One should conceive the great notion of terror toward the wheel of conditioned phenomena and afflictions;
the notion of enemies toward the aggregates;
and the notion of an empty house toward the sense bases.
One should regard the various elements as being like venomous snakes;
the three realms as being characterized by decay and affliction;
and nirvana as being characterized by benefit and peace.
He contemplates all sensual desires as being like spittle or mucus, deeply delights in the life of renunciation, and does not contravene the Buddha’s teachings.
Toward sentient beings, he exhorts them to practice merit; toward all worlds, he no longer harbors a defiled mind.

One perceives all Buddhas as manifesting before oneself; one receives all bodies as being like illusions or dreams; one observes and eliminates all marks; and through contemplation, one does not perceive coming and going across the three periods of time.

With pure faith, they have deep conviction in the true and wondrous; they contemplate all Buddhas as equal throughout the three periods of time, remaining unshakable while able to uphold all roots of goodness.
They possess sovereign mastery over the samādhis of all Buddhas, yet they are ultimately never stained by or attached to the physical marks of the Buddhas.
Regarding all phenomena as entirely equal, they do not contend with anything in the world.

They act in accordance with what ought to be done without contradiction, penetrate the profound twelve links of dependent origination, exhaustively master all stages of the Tathāgatas' path, and attain supreme patience to enter the true realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*).

One perceives that the nature of the realm of sentient beings is without arising or ceasing; one perceives that the realm of nirvāṇa is primordially manifest. With the pure eye of wisdom, one contemplates all phenomena as non-dual.
That bodhicitta has neither center nor periphery, and the essence of all Buddhas is without differentiation.
Entering the gate of unimpeded, pure wisdom, one clearly perceives the natural awakening-wisdom of bodhi.
One conceives of spiritual friends as Buddhas and does not entertain thoughts of separation from Bodhisattvas.
Having already destroyed the armies of Māra within the cycle of birth and death, one should regard all phenomena as being like transformations.
Seeing all Tathāgatas as reflections in a mirror, one should seek that bodhicitta.
"All the pāramitās are without exception equal; the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is inexhaustible, gathering the merits of the Buddhas.
"Worthy Protector!
This is the Bodhisattva’s samādhi of contemplating all Buddhas as manifest before one."
If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to fully accomplish such a samādhi, they should first accomplish such merits.
Kalyāṇamitra, you should know that there are further immeasurable merits, which likewise arise in dependence upon this samādhi.
The Buddha again addressed Bhadrapāla, saying:
"Among these, what samādhi is able to give rise to such meritorious practices?
It is the so-called 'Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddhas as Present Before One' that is able to give rise to such meritorious dharmas."
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
What is called the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddhas Appearing Before One?
Bhadrapāla!"
If there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who maintain the precepts with purity and are fully endowed with all practices, dwelling alone in a secluded place, they should reflect thus:
"In every location, in whichever direction it may be, where is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha in the Western Quarter?"
At that time, having heard what he has heard, that person should immediately form this reflection within themselves: "As I have heard:
that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha is now in the western direction; passing beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-fields from here, there is a world named Sukhāvatī."
"In this way, the Tathāgata now currently dwells there, surrounded on all sides by bodhisattvas, teaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings within the great assembly.

Because that person relies upon what they have heard, fixing their mindfulness, contemplating, and observing without ceasing until it becomes clear and distinct, they will ultimately succeed in seeing that Amitābha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

It is as if, in this world, a man or a woman, while in a dream, sees various things—namely gold, silver, many jewels, precious wealth, and storehouses; or sees friends and acquaintances; or sees those whom they find unpleasant when awake. Whatever objects the person encounters in that dream, whether adverse or favorable, whether causing sorrow or joy—at times they speak with extreme delight and pleasure, and at times they are agitated and distressed, grieving to the depths of their hearts. After waking, the person reflects upon and remembers them, proclaiming to others at length what was seen in the dream, and by recollecting the dream, they experience sorrow and joy."
In this way, Bhadrapāla!

Those sons of good family and daughters of good family sit upright with focused mindfulness, concentrating their thoughts on that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha—on his such physical marks and signs, such majestic deportment, such assembly, and such preaching of the Dharma.

If one maintains mindfulness as heard, with single-minded continuity in an orderly sequence without distraction—whether for a single day, a single night, or even up to seven days and seven nights—then because of possessing the full mindfulness of what was previously heard, this person will certainly behold the Tathāgata Amitābha, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"If you cannot see him during the daytime, then Amitābha Buddha will certainly appear during the night or within a dream.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

For example, suppose a man or a woman in this world travels far away to another country and, in the midst of sleep, sees their own home; at that time, they truly do not know whether it is day or night, nor do they know whether they are inside or outside.
At that time, whatever eye-faculty this person possesses cannot be obstructed by walls, fences, or rocky mountains; even in the depths of the gloom and pitch-black darkness, it shall not be hindered.

“Bhadrapāla! It is likewise with the unobstructed mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. When they maintain right mindfulness, all the Sumeru Kings, as well as the Cakravāḍa Mountains, Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, and even all other Black Mountains that exist throughout the intervals between those buddha-fields, cannot act as obstructions for their faculty of sight, nor can they obscure this mind.”

However, this person has not actually attained the divine eye to see that Buddha, nor the divine ear to hear his Dharma-sounds; they have not traveled to that world by means of supernatural powers, nor have they passed away from this world to be reborn before that Buddha. Rather, it is simply because they have accumulated mindfulness and cultivated their practice within this very world, observing with long-standing clarity and sharpness, that they ultimately succeed in beholding that Tathāgata Amitābha, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded by a multitude of monks and bodhisattvas. They may see themselves there listening to the Dharma, and having heard it, they remember, uphold, and practice it;
or at times, they further succeed in reverently bowing to, honoring, and making offerings to that Tathāgata Amitābha, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Only after this can such a person give rise to this samādhi;
having emerged from contemplation, they reflect in successive order and extensively explain for others what they have seen and heard.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"
Thus, there were three men in the kingdom of Magadha:

the first heard that in the city of Vaiśālī there was a courtesan named Sumana; the second heard that there was a courtesan named Āmrapālī; and the third heard that there was a courtesan named Utpalavarṇā.
Having heard this, each of them devised skillful means and applied their minds with diligent pursuit, never ceasing for even a moment.
Yet, those three men had never actually seen such women; it was merely through hearing of them from afar that they gave rise to lustful thoughts, which they focused upon without ceasing.
After that dream, he will engage in sexual intercourse with that woman in Rājagṛha;
once the act is completed, his desire will subside and his longing will be fulfilled, whereupon he will awaken.

Upon waking, he will recall what occurred in the dream—just as it was heard and seen, and just as it was experienced—and will come to you to relate it all in detail. You should then skillfully teach him the Dharma and guide him accordingly, so that he may abide in the stage of non-retrogression and ultimately achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

In the future, he will surely attain Buddhahood, known by the name Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, titled "Sujñāna" (Well-Awakened).
In this way, once these three persons had attained patience (*kṣānti*), they again recalled their past lives with perfect clarity. "Bhadrapāla!

It is likewise for those sons and daughters of good family who wish to accomplish the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva samādhi of contemplating all Buddhas as manifest before them. While their bodies remain constantly in this world, if they briefly hear the name of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha, and are able to fix their minds upon it in continuous contemplation—uninterrupted and orderly—they will clearly behold that Buddha Amitābha. This is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation, the complete accomplishment of the samādhi of all Buddhas manifest before one."
Because he was able to see the Buddha through this samādhi, he then questioned that Amitābha Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By accomplishing what dharmas do the various bodhisattvas attain birth within this buddha-field?"
At that time, Amitābha Buddha spoke to these bodhisattvas, saying:
"If a person resolves their mind to seek birth here, they should always bind their thoughts to right mindfulness, maintaining it in continuous succession toward Amitābha Buddha;

then they shall attain birth. Once they have attained birth, the World-Honored One, knowing their mind, will likewise keep them in mind, and only then will they behold the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
"O Bhadrapāla! At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha addressed those people, saying:
'O sons of good family!'"
"You should cultivate with right mindfulness and diligent effort, and give rise to a vast mind; you will certainly be born there.
"Bhadrapāla! At that time, that bodhisattva again addressed Amitābha Buddha, saying:"
“World-Honored One!
How should one practice mindfulness of the Buddha, World-Honored One, diligently cultivating it and giving rise to a vast mind so as to be born in this land?
“Bhadrapāla! [the Buddha replied.]
Then Amitābha Buddha again addressed them, saying:
"Sons of good family!
If you now wish to practice the correct mindfulness of the Buddha, you should contemplate him in this way:
"Now, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha,
Bhagavān Amitābha is endowed with these thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, and his body..."

His physical radiance was like a mass of molten gold; he was fully endowed with and seated upon a magnificent jeweled palanquin, emitting great light as he sat upon a lion throne. Amidst the assembly of śramaṇas, he preached this Dharma:
"That which is spoken of refers to the fact that all dharmas are fundamentally indestructible and there is no destroyer. This is as with indestructible form, and so on..."
Because they do not destroy the aggregates such as consciousness; and likewise, because they do not destroy the great elements from earth up to wind;
and again, because they do not destroy the sense bases from form up to touch;
and furthermore, because they do not destroy [beings] from Brahmā up to all the lords of the world.
"In this way, up to not recollecting that Tathāgata and not apprehending that Tathāgata.
Having formed such a thought regarding the Tathāgata, he thus successively attained the *śūnyatā-samādhi*.
"Good son! This is called the Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of All Buddhas through Right Mindfulness. "Bhadrapāla!"

At that time, when that bodhisattva has arisen from samādhi and comes to you to inquire about the characteristics of this samādhi, you should immediately preach the Dharma to him and provide instruction in accordance with his needs, so that he may attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Scripture of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, Scroll One;
The Great Vaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, Section on Bhadrapāla, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter One, Part Two: On Contemplation.
"Bhadrapāla! At that time, I likewise bestowed upon that Buddha the prediction of his future enlightenment."
This person shall in the future certainly attain Buddhahood, being named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, up to Buddha, World-Honored One, called Virtue-Radiance (Guṇaprabhāsa).
“Bhadrapāla! Who shall witness and know this samādhi within it?
My disciples Mahākāśyapa, the Bodhisattva Śakradeva, the Devaputra Bhadraguṇa, and countless other bodhisattvas—all of whom have already cultivated and attained this samādhi—are its witnesses.”
How is it realized?
It is what is called the samādhi of emptiness. "Bhadrapāla!
I recall that in the past there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Subhāṣita.

At that time, there was a man who encountered a vast wilderness; distressed by hunger and thirst, he eventually fell asleep. In his dream, he obtained all kinds of exquisite and superior foods; having eaten his fill, he was no longer hungry or parched.
Upon waking from this sleep, however, he was once again hungry and thirsty.
Because of this, the person reflects to himself:
"In this way, all phenomena are empty and without reality; they are like what is seen in a dream, fundamentally not true."
"When one contemplates in this manner, one awakens to the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) and attains non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus it is, Bhadrapāla!"

There are bodhisattvas—whether householders or renunciants—who, upon hearing that there are Buddhas in any particular direction, immediately pay homage with a sincere heart toward that direction. With a mind of thirsty longing desiring to see those Buddhas, they engage in such focused contemplation;
furthermore, they should contemplate the physical marks and signs [of the Buddhas] while simultaneously forming the perception of space.
Once they have accomplished this perception of space, they abide in such right contemplation.
Having dwelled in such contemplation, one attains the vision of that Buddha’s radiance, as transparent and clear as pure lapis lazuli, and his form, as upright and majestic as a pillar of pure gold.
For one who contemplates in this way, the vision of the Tathāgata is likewise so.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

It is as if there were a person who suddenly departs from his native land for another region; although he is in that other region, he constantly recollects his original place of birth—having seen it thus, heard it thus, remembered it thus, and understood it thus."
Due to long-standing recollection, he clearly sees himself within a dream in his place of birth, experiencing and perceiving things exactly as they were previously encountered.
At a later time, this person relates the events seen in the dream to his kinsmen, saying:
"I saw such-and-such; I heard such-and-such; I performed such-and-such actions; and I obtained such-and-such."
"In this way, Bhadrapāla!

There are bodhisattvas—whether householders or renunciants—who, upon hearing from another that there is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, in whichever direction he may dwell, immediately face that direction and prostrate with a sincere heart. Desiring to see that Buddha with undistracted right mindfulness, they shall see the image of that Buddha as soon as they think of it—appearing either like lapis lazuli or pure gold. It is just so."
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

It is as if a bhikṣu practices the contemplation of impurity and beholds a freshly dead corpse whose form and color have just begun to change—whether it be blue, yellow, black, or red; or at times swollen, or already putrefied, with pus and blood flowing together, being devoured by insects and beasts, until the flesh is gone and the bones are white, their color like that of a conch shell, continuing in this manner until he contemplates the bones scattered apart."
Yet those scattered bones come from nowhere and go nowhere; they are produced solely by the mind, and one thus perceives them as one's own mind.
"In this way, Bhadrapāla! [he said].

If bodhisattvas wish to achieve that samādhi in which the Buddhas appear before them, in whichever direction they first intend to see those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, they shall see the Tathāgatas immediately in the very place where they have directed their thoughts.
Why is this? One attains the vision of the Tathāgata through the samādhi of causes and conditions.
There are three causes and conditions for attaining the vision of that Buddha.
What are these three?
First, being conditioned by this samādhi; second, the empowerment of those Buddhas; and third, the ripening of one's own roots of goodness.
Because they are fully endowed with these three causes and conditions, they likewise obtain clear vision of all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

Suppose there is a person in the prime of youth, with a handsome and dignified appearance, who wishes to observe whether his own form is beautiful or ugly, fair or foul. He would then take a vessel, fill it with clear oil, or hold pure water, or take a crystal, or grasp a bright mirror; using these four things, he observes the reflection of his face, and its beauty, ugliness, fairness, or foulness appears clearly and distinctly."
Bhadrapāla! What do you think?
When that reflected image appears within these four locations—oil, water, crystal, and a bright mirror—does it exist prior to appearing there?
Bhadrapāla replied, "No. He asked:
"Was this originally non-existent? He replied, "No."
He asked, "Is this within? He replied:
"No, it is not. He said, "In that case,
does it perhaps exist outside?"
He replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”

It is only because those substances—oil, water, crystal, and mirror—are clear and bright, free from turbidity and impurity, that when a form stands before them, its reflection appears accordingly; yet that appearing image does not emerge from those four substances, nor does it come from any other place; it is neither spontaneously existent nor created by a person.
"You should know that those images come from nowhere, go nowhere, and have no arising, no ceasing, and no place of abiding.
When Bhadrapāla had answered thus, the Buddha said, "Bhadrapāla!"
It is so, it is so. Just as you have said, when all things are pure, their forms become luminous and images manifest of themselves without requiring much effort.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: with a single-minded and skillful thought, he beholds all the Tathāgatas; having seen them, he abides; having abided, he inquires about the meaning;
having received the explanation, he rejoices. He then further reflects: "From where has this Buddha come?"
From where, then, has this body of mine emerged?
Upon observing that Tathāgata, I find he has no place of coming or going;
my own body is likewise: fundamentally there is no emerging or departing, so how could there be any returning?
He should further reflect in this way:
"Now, these three realms exist solely as mind. Why is this?"
Following that thought, one returns to see the mind itself.

Now, I have seen the Buddha through the mind; my mind creates the Buddha, my mind is the Buddha. My mind is the Tathāgata, my mind is my own body, and my mind sees the Buddha. Yet the mind does not know the mind, nor does the mind see the mind. When the mind possesses conceptualization, it constitutes birth and death; when the mind is free from conceptualization, it is nirvāṇa.
"All phenomena are not real; they arise through thought and conditions. Once that which is thought has ceased, the thinker is also empty.
O Bhadrapāla, you should know that it is by means of this samādhi that all bodhisattvas realize great enlightenment.

Chapter 2: On the Practice of Samādhi. From the *Bhadrapāla-parivarta* of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, Chapter Two: On the Practice of Samādhi. At that time, the Blessed One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla, saying: “Bhadrapāla!”
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fully practice four dharmas, they will be able to attain this samādhi of presence before one.
What are these four?
First, not undermining faith; second, not breaking diligence; third, excellence of wisdom; and fourth, drawing near to virtuous friends.
"Bhadrapāla!
These are the four dharmas which, when fully possessed by a bodhisattva, lead to the accomplishment of the samādhi of presence. Bhadrapāla!"
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through their complete practice, can achieve the samādhi of presence before one’s eyes.
What are these four?
First, not to have even a single thought of a sentient being for as long as a kṣaṇa.
Second, not to sleep for even a moment during the three months;
third, to practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) for three months, except for the time of relieving oneself;
fourth, when giving the Dharma at mealtime, to do so without seeking fame or profit, and with no expectation of reward.
"Bhadrapāla!
These are the four dharmas which, when fully possessed by a bodhisattva, lead to the accomplishment of the samādhi of presence. Bhadrapāla!"

Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through practicing them fully, attains the accomplishment of the samādhi of presence before one's eyes (*pratyutpanna-samādhi*). What are these four?
First, exhorting others to see the Buddha; second, teaching people to listen to the Dharma; third, having no envy or jealousy in one’s mind; and fourth, exhorting others to resolve upon bodhicitta.
"Bhadrapāla!
These are the four dharmas which, when fully possessed by a bodhisattva, lead to the accomplishment of the samādhi of presence. Bhadrapāla!"
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes samādhi.
What are these four?
First, to fashion images of the Buddha and encourage others to practice offerings to them.
Second, to transcribe this sutra and cause others to read and recite it;
third, to instruct sentient beings who are arrogant toward the Dharma to resolve their minds for enlightenment;
fourth, to protect and uphold the true Dharma so that it may endure for a long time.
"Bhadrapāla!
These are the four dharmas which, when fully possessed by a bodhisattva, lead to the accomplishment of the Samādhi of Presence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"You should all abide within the Buddha-dharma; do not conceal the true words or my teaching.
Mindfully exert yourselves with diligence to remove the hindrance of drowsiness; for three months, do not sit, but practice walking meditation alone."
When eating, he speaks extensively to bestow upon others, proclaiming the peerless Dharma of all Buddhas;
seeking neither fame nor gain, because he is free from attachment, he attains this dhyāna.
Do not give rise to jealousy or anger; you should contemplate the mind that seeks liberation from all desires.
Those who delight in this samādhi and seek to abide in it will attain it through diligent mindfulness without indolence.
With a golden body adorned by a hundred merits, Elegant and perfect like a flower in full bloom,
A physical form of radiant light that the world delights to behold— May I always behold all Buddhas appearing before me.
To all the Buddhas of the past, those of the future, and all those supreme among humans in the present—
bow down with single-minded reverence and always cultivate offerings with focused mindfulness.
If you were to make offerings to those Buddhas, using flowers, incense, and ointments,
and with a pure mind giving excellent food through the gift of wisdom, it would not be difficult at all to realize this samādhi.
Before the stupas of all Buddhas, they perform various musical offerings—conchs, drums, gongs, and bells with their wondrous sounds;
with joy and leaping exultation beyond measure, they shall surely achieve this samādhi.
Exhort others to create images of the Peerless Body, Adorned with painted colors and complete marks, With golden light, vast and free from blemish;
For such a one, it is not difficult to realize this samādhi.
Each and every one should constantly practice the gift of Dharma, Purely uphold the prohibitive precepts, and cultivate extensive learning;
With diligent and courageous effort, eliminate all indolence, And before long, you shall attain this samādhi.
One should not harbor a poisonous mind toward others, nor should one abandon the various desires of the world;
by always regarding all beings with compassion, how could samādhi be far off—it will manifest before you.
Always rejoice in the presence of the Dharma Master, honoring and respecting him as you would the Tathāgata;
do not give rise to contempt or stinginess, but offer worship with a joyful heart, free from envy.
Innumerable Buddhas together extol it; you need only seek it with diligence and it shall naturally be attained.
The World-Honored One has solemnly expounded this for the sake of practicing such a wondrous Dharma.

3. Chapter on Seeing the Buddha. The *Bhadracarī-praṇidhāna* Section of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, Chapter Three: Seeing the Buddha. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying: “Bhadrapāla!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to achieve this samādhi, they should conceive of that Dharma-preacher as a Buddha and give rise to a heart of reverence; they must not harbor arrogance, nor any thoughts of contention, opposition, or non-compliance. Only after doing so may they diligently practice and study this supreme samādhi, whereby they will finally be able to realize it.

“Bhadrapāla! If a person conceives unwholesome thoughts, a mind of contrariness, a mind of contention, a mind of intentional humiliation, or various impure thoughts toward that Dharma-preaching Dharma-master or bhikṣu, and fails even to give rise to the perception of him as being like the Buddhas—then such a bodhisattva, even if they were to practice, would ultimately never be able to realize such a sublime samādhi; it is impossible for them to realize it.”

“Bhadrapāla! It is like the pure, cloudless sky; when a person with clear vision gazes into the sky at a quiet night, they can distinguish the immeasurable stars within it, perceiving their various locations and distinct forms with perfect clarity.”

In this way, Bhadrapāla, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that dharmic nature as empty space, they see all the Tathāgatas through the perfection of their mental conception; such is the manner of this matter.

"When that bodhisattva contemplates the eastern direction, he frequently sees many Buddhas—frequently seeing a hundred Buddhas, frequently seeing a thousand Buddhas, frequently seeing a hundred thousand Buddhas, frequently seeing a billion Buddhas, frequently seeing a hundred thousand billion Buddhas, and frequently seeing a hundred thousand nayuta billion Buddhas—all appearing naturally before him without the need for deliberate mental application."

Once that bodhisattva has thus observed the eastern direction, he next observes the southern, western, and northern directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir—the ten directions of the world-systems—in each of which he sees many Buddhas: namely, he sees many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many millions of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of Buddhas—all appearing before him without the need for any deliberate effort.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

Just as those bodhisattvas in the world of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha who are born in that land, on the first day observe the eastern direction and see many Buddhas—seeing many hundreds of Buddhas, and even seeing many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas—and only after that, on the second day, observe the southern direction, and so on for all ten directions; in every case, it is just like this."
In this way, Bhadrapāla!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the bodhisattva samādhi of the manifestation of all buddhas before one’s eyes, such a bodhisattva, while observing the ten directions within his own land, frequently sees many buddhas—frequently seeing a hundred buddhas, and even frequently seeing hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of buddhas.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
Just as all Tathāgatas achieve the Buddha-eye, having thus attained it, they know and see everything in all places exactly as it is."
In this way, Bhadrapāla!

Once a bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished the bodhisattva samādhi of the presence of all buddhas before one's eyes, they naturally fulfill that perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā), up to and including fulfilling all the various merits of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Just as when the clouds and mist have cleared from a tranquil night, one with clear vision looks up at the sky and sees those many stars,
numbering more than a hundred thousand, and remembers them clearly even during the day without any loss."
Once the bodhisattva has thus attained this samādhi, he beholds many billions of buddhas;
thereafter, upon arising from this samādhi, he again expounds the most honored Dharma for the great assembly.
Just as my Buddha-eye is pure, seeing the world without any obstruction,
so too is this Bodhisattva-eye of the sons of the Buddhas, which issues forth from this samādhi as the most supreme vision.
Contemplating the Tathāgata through the perception of signlessness, one beholds all the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the ten directions;
having destroyed afflictions, poisons, and all conceptualizations, listen now to the wondrous merits of the Bodhisattva.
If one listens to that Dharma with a cool and serene mind, one can enter the state of emptiness and stillness, free from fear;
as I now preach this Dharma, it is for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to realize Bodhi.
Just as those bodhisattvas dwelling in bliss see many immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
so too do these bodhisattvas, entering into contemplation, see hundreds of thousands of many Tamer-Controllers.
In this way, only Ānanda among the bhikṣus can receive everything upon hearing me speak;
likewise, when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they can hear all dharmas and maintain them in total retention.
Having accomplished faith and a sense of shame, and being endowed with samādhi, one completely abandons all worldly speech;
always teaching others with a heart of loving-kindness and wisdom, one shall surely reach this state of tranquility.

Chapter Four: Right Faith. From the *Bhadrapāla-parivarta* of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, Chapter Four: Right Faith. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying: “Bhadrapāla!”
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek such a jewel of samādhi, they should rouse courageous and diligent effort; thus, they will naturally and swiftly be able to enter this samādhi.

“Bhadrapāla! It is like a person who boards a great ship and enters the vast ocean, filling it to his heart’s content with all manner of exquisite treasures, having already passed through all the great perils and being on the verge of reaching this shore.”
Before long, the ship suddenly broke apart and the multitude of treasures sank.
At that moment, the people of Jambudvīpa raised a great cry and gave rise to profound sorrow and suffering, for they had lost such priceless jewels.

“Bhadrapāla! It is the same for good sons and good daughters who, upon hearing of such a supreme jewel of a samādhi with their own ears, are unable to write it down, recite it, or uphold it; nor can they contemplate it or abide in accordance with the Dharma.”
Bhadrapāla!
You should know that at that time, all the devas and other celestial beings of the world will likewise raise great cries and give rise to profound sorrow and distress, saying:
"These sentient beings are truly to be pitied."

Why is it that when a bodhisattva hears of these supreme jewels of samādhi of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—which are praised by all Buddhas, authorized by all Buddhas, instructed by all Buddhas, and which constitute the most supreme merit of all Buddhas, fully accomplished and perfectly complete without deficiency—they instead distance themselves from them after hearing of them, being unwilling to transcribe them, taking no pleasure in reading or reciting them, being unable to receive and uphold them, explain their meaning and principles, contemplate them, or abide in accordance with the Dharma?
“Thus, sentient beings who are heedless and indolent will certainly suffer great decline in the future.
“Bhadrapāla! What is meant by the decline of sentient beings?”

That which is called "diminution" refers to having heard this jewel-like samādhi and yet remaining distant from it; being unable to write it down, recite it, or uphold it; being unable to explain it or contemplate its meaning; failing to abide in accordance with the Dharma and practicing with focused mindfulness; and thus causing one's merits to perish—this is what constitutes diminution.
"Bhadrapāla!
It is impossible for those who are indolent or those who are wicked beings to obtain any benefit from this Dharma.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

For example, suppose someone were to take red sandalwood and show it to a foolish person; because of his folly, that foolish person would perceive the fragrance of the red sandalwood as a foul and putrid odor.
Then the wise man who was selling the sandalwood said to the foolish man:
"You should not now conceive a notion of foulness toward this exquisite sandalwood. Why is that?
"This almsgiving is most refined, its fragrance supreme.
For what reason do you now regard it as foul and evil?
If you do not believe me, you should first smell and taste it to see whether it is foul or fragrant."
Furthermore, since your eyes are clear, you should also use them to observe whether the color and patterns of this *tán* light are emaciated or plump, auspicious or inauspicious.

"Yet that fool, despite hearing such words from the wise man and their various praises, because of his ignorance, instead gives rise to hatred; he pinches his nose with his hand so as not to smell, and covers his eyes, refusing to look."
"In this way, Bhadrapāla!
In future ages there will be wicked bhikṣus who harbor hatred for this sutra; their conduct will be just like that.
Those wicked people do not know how to cultivate bodily precepts, mental discipline, or wisdom; they are foolish and ignorant, like white rams—stupid, dull-witted, and perverse."

Furthermore, because those evil persons lack merit, although they may hear this sublime scripture—the Samādhi of Right Mindfulness on the Buddhas Appearing Before One—they do not transcribe it, cannot recite it, cannot receive and uphold it, cannot contemplate it, cannot proclaim and explain it extensively for others, and furthermore, cannot give rise to extensive sympathetic joy; how then could they possibly practice according to what is taught?
If those evil persons were able to speak of the practice, such a thing would be impossible.

Furthermore, having heard it, they would instead give rise to slander; possessing no faith at all, they would claim it to be false, and though they hear many explanations, they will ultimately never attain understanding.
They further spoke these words:

"If this Dharma were merely for the sake of frivolous discourse, they would have performed miracles; or if it were for the sake of propagating their teachings, they would have embellished their words excessively. They have composed this scripture to delude and deceive the world. How could it possibly be compared to the various sūtras proclaimed by the noble Ānanda and the assembly of bhikṣus while they were still present in this world?"
Furthermore, at another time, he spoke these words:
"This sūtra was not spoken by the Buddha; it is merely a composition created by wicked men, falsely claiming to be a scripture."
“Bhadrapāla, you should know this:
such evil persons remain far removed for a long night from this subtle, wondrous, and unsurpassed great jewel;
they are like that foolish man who, upon seeing exquisite fragrance, covers his eyes and blocks his nose, refusing to see or smell it.”
Thus it is, Bhadrapāla!

When those foolish and wicked people hear this wondrous sūtra, this jewel of samādhi, they do not wish to copy it, do not delight in reading or reciting it, do not contemplate or uphold it, and are unable to proclaim it—namely, because they have no intention to draw near to it and have no desire to hear it.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
It is as if there were a person selling a maṇi jewel, and a foolish person, having seen that jewel, immediately asked:
'O worthy one!'"
"What is the value of this treasure?

The owner of the treasure replied, "You should know now that this treasure is exquisite and supreme, such as does not exist in the world; it cannot be discussed with worldly prices in a casual manner."
I shall now briefly describe, in general terms, the efficacy, majesty, and power of this jewel.
If you wish to know how far the light of this maṇi-jewel extends, and if you require it, you must cover this ground entirely with pure gold; only then will I give it to you.
When that foolish person heard these words, he laughed loudly and disparaged them in various ways, saying:
"This mani-jewel has not been paid for at all."
"In this way, Bhadrapāla!

Those evil bhikṣus of the future world, upon hearing of this supreme samādhi-treasure within this sūtra, will lack faith, frequently give rise to derision, and further incite slander; their conduct shall be just like that."

“Or there may be a bhikṣu whose faculty of faith is profound and thick, and whose faculty of wisdom is clear and sharp; one who, in the presence of past Tathāgatas, has drawn near and served them, heard the true Dharma, practiced according to the teaching, and planted various roots of goodness.”

Upon hearing this Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Manifestation of Mindfulness of the Buddha, they will immediately be able to recite it, contemplate its meaning, explain it extensively for others, and bring great benefit to all the world—meaning that they will widely proclaim and disseminate it; they will give rise to great faith and develop great wisdom, achieve purity and straightforwardness, and be endowed with dignified deportment; they will constantly practice shame and remorse, fear all transgressions, cultivate and maintain the prohibitive precepts, and refrain from all desires; they will believe in the profound Dharma and be able to hear much of it, attain deep intellectual patience, and constantly practice loving-kindness and compassion; yet, these individuals must have roots of faith that are firm and solid to obtain this samādhi.
Having attained this samādhi, he traveled through various regions and countries, extensively expounding and explaining its principles for others, while constantly making this vow:
"May this profound sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha be widely circulated and remain forever in the world."

"Furthermore, there may be sentient beings whose roots of goodness are feeble and whose merit is meager; who in the past have never drawn near to the Buddhas, made offerings, served them, or heard the True Dharma; but rather, being overcome by self-conceit, led astray by envy, shrouded by gain and profit, and dragged along by fame, they practice extensive negligence, do not maintain the virtues of the precepts, constantly delight in a distracted mind, do not cultivate meditative concentration, distance themselves from the scriptural teachings, and do not seek extensive learning; they have not encountered virtuous teachers but have only met with evil friends."

Such a person, having heard this samādhi, slanders and reviles it; lacking even a single grain of faith, they claim it is untrue, their disposition being stubborn and ignorant, their minds devoid of understanding.
Furthermore, they shall say:

"A scripture such as this was not spoken by the Buddha; rather, it is a composition written by dull-witted bhikṣus of the world, who, out of ignorance and false views, have themselves fashioned these words and embellished the phrasing."
If you are among a multitude, you should speak thus and instruct them in this way:
"You sentient beings should know that this sūtra scripture was not spoken by the Buddha."

"Thus, such deluded persons do not know how to draw near to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; they do not plant roots of goodness nor cultivate offerings. They associate with evil friends and commit many evils. You should know that such people remain far removed from the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous Dharma-treasure, and will forever lose the benefit of the unsurpassed, most supreme Dharma."
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"I speak to you again:

while I am now proclaiming this wondrous samādhi before the great assembly of all the worlds—Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others—if those sons or daughters of good family, having heard it, rejoice in it, read and recite it, receive and uphold it, contemplate and believe in the Buddha-samādhi, regarding it as the most true, and utter these words:"
"One who speaks thus of the true teachings of all Buddhas should be known to have acquired an inconceivable mass of merit,
O Bhadrapāla!"

Furthermore, if there are good sons or good daughters who take various kinds of precious jewels filling a trichiliocosm and use them to make offerings to all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, although the merit they obtain is vast and great, it does not equal even one hundred-thousand-millionth part of the mass of merit obtained from upholding this sutra; indeed, even an immeasurable, boundless, and asaṃkhyeya mass of merit would still not equal it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses: "Those who are crooked,
foolish, and deluded, Whose faculties are immature due to negligence,
Ruined by evil friends, And who possess no right faith."
Having broken the precepts and committed many transgressions, they were deeply attached to their own conceit,
each saying: "This sutra was not spoken by the Buddhas."
"These various sūtras are not the teachings of the Dharma King.
Those people, according to their own views, say:
"How could we possibly speak of these?"
If one sees the Great Tamer, the World-Honored One, emitting radiance,
I shall proclaim it extensively for him, and he too will be able to transmit it.
Should anyone, upon hearing this sutra, give rise to joy,
This person is free from the net of doubt;
they do not say, "This was not spoken by the Buddha.
If their precepts are pure, they will be able to clearly understand what they perceive.
Out of reverence for the Dharma, I have developed a profound resolve and shall now explain it for you.
Even if one were to take three thousand precious jewels and offer them to all the Tathāgatas in pursuit of Great Bodhi, that merit would be beyond description.
"If there are bhikṣus who preach the concentration praised by the Buddha, and those who hear it give rise to faith, this merit exceeds that [of the former].

Chapter Five: Receiving and Upholding The *Bhadrapāla-bodhisattva-parivarta* of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, Chapter Five: Receiving and Upholding. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying:

“Bhadrapāla! Among this assembly, there are those who have now heard me personally preach this samādhi before my presence. After my parinirvāṇa, wherever they are reborn, they shall once again hear this treasure of a samādhi; yet, though they hear it, they will not believe it, but will instead slander and revile it, distance themselves from virtuous friends, and follow after evil people.”

“Bhadrapāla! Furthermore, there may be a person who, having heard this profound and wondrous sūtra on samādhi from a virtuous person, still does not give rise to faith, does not regard it as true, and is unable to understand it—how much less could one who hears this sūtra in the presence of an evil person give rise to faith and further understand it?”
Why is this? Bhadrapāla!
The words spoken by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are difficult to believe, for the wisdom of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is difficult to know.
"Bhadrapāla!
If one should accomplish such a samādhi, only then will one be able to cause the Buddha-dharma to increase for all sentient beings in future ages.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—whether lay or ordained—who, upon hearing this samādhi, do not fear, are not startled, do not regret, do not retreat, do not slander, and do not disparage it; having heard it, they rejoice, give rise to a mind of faith and reverence, become certain of its truth without further webs of doubt, and read, recite, uphold, and contemplate its meaning and intent.
"Bhadrapāla!
Such persons as these are all seen, all known, and all recognized by the World-Honored One. Bhadrapāla!"
How do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perceive these good sons and good daughters?
Furthermore, how do they know them, and how do they recognize them?
Bhadrapāla!
