If one can read, recite, receive, uphold, and contemplate this gate of samādhi, such a person will never commit evil, will not break the pure precepts, will not destroy right faith, and will not enter the assembly of the heterodox.
Bhadrapāla!

These sons and daughters of good family will certainly possess deep faith and achieve contemplation, and they will be able to achieve analytical contemplation; they will be fully endowed with faith in this Dharma and shall constantly be able to read, recite, and uphold it.
Bhadrapāla, you should know that such a person certainly does not seek meager merit, nor do they plant meager roots of goodness.
Bhadrapāla!
Wherever these sons or daughters of good family are born, even if they may lack material necessities, their roots of goodness are vast and not small.
“Bhadrapāla! Therefore, these sons and daughters of good family have already practiced, made offerings, and planted roots of goodness in the presence of the Tathāgatas of the past.”

Bhadrapāla, you should know that these people have not planted roots of goodness by practicing and making offerings to a single Tathāgata; nor have they planted roots of goodness under two, three, four, five, or even ten Tathāgatas; nor have they planted roots of goodness under hundreds, thousands, or billions of Tathāgatas.

Bhadrapāla, you should know that these sons and daughters of good family have already practiced, made offerings, and planted roots of goodness before countless, boundless Tathāgatas numbering more than hundreds of thousands; only then do they hear this Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of the Buddha.
Having heard it, they give rise to faith, their minds open and their understanding clear, taking it as reality without further webs of doubt.
Once they have heard it, they delight in copying, reciting, upholding, and even extensively proclaiming its meaning for others.
Why is this? Bhadrapāla!
These sons and daughters of good family have, in the past, already heard this samādhi before the Tathāgatas, and have read, recited, received, and upheld it.

For this reason, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, at the very end of the final five hundred years—when the Dharma is about to perish and the Dharma is on the verge of destruction—one shall still hear of such a samādhi; upon hearing it, one will immediately give rise to faith, without alarm or doubt, without falling back or sinking, and with great joy filling the body and mind, one shall read, recite, receive, uphold, contemplate its meaning, explain it to others, and even practice this samādhi for a single day and night.

“Bhadrapāla! If there should be another person who, upon hearing this samādhi, feels no alarm or fear, does not fall back or sink away, and does not give rise to slander; who, having heard it, rejoices in it as being true, reflects upon it with discernment, and attains clarity and understanding in mind; and who can even for a brief moment praise it as excellent to others—the mass of merit they obtain would still be immeasurable. How much more so for one who can read, recite, receive, and uphold it, practice it with diligent reflection, and explain it extensively to others for even a single day and night?”

Bhadrapāla, you should know that because of this matter, these sons and daughters of good family will immediately obtain a mass of great merit exceeding immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and they shall thereafter abide in the stage of non-retrogression, such that whatever they wish for is accomplished according to their desire.
“Bhadrapāla! Although that is so, I shall now further proclaim a parable for you to clarify this meaning.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!”

Suppose, for example, there were a person who took all the great earth of this trichiliocosm and ground it entirely into dust; furthermore, they took all grasses, trees, branches, and leaves—regardless of whether they were large or small—and reduced them all to fine particles.

At that time, the person would take a single particle from that heap of dust, break it down and analyze it, and cause it to become as many particles as there originally were; thereafter, they would again take all those particles and sequentially divide them until their number was equal to that of the original single particle.
"Bhadrapāla!
What do you think?
Can the number of these atoms be said to be many?"
Bhadrapāla replied, “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said, “Bhadrapāla!

Suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who took as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in those aforementioned [fields], filled them completely with various jewels, and offered them as a gift.”
"Bhadrapāla!
What do you think?
Is the mass of merit obtained by those sons and daughters of good family not even greater?"
Bhadrapāla replied,
“It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"Nevertheless, because of this matter, those sons and daughters of good family shall obtain a mass of merit that surpasses that immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable [mass of merit].
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Bhadrapāla!"

I shall tell you further: if those sons or daughters of good family were to take as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms of dust and fill them with the seven treasures to offer as a gift, they would obtain such merit;

yet, if another son or daughter of good family, upon hearing of this Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of Mindfulness of the Buddha, should for a moment give rise to sympathetic joy, believe with faith and discern it as true, have their minds opened and their intentions resolved, read and recite it, receive and uphold it, or even briefly explain it to others—the mass of merit obtained by these sons or daughters of good family surpasses the merit of the former offering, being immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, incomparable, and beyond the reach of thought.
Bhadrapāla!

Thus, if a son or daughter of good family, upon hearing this samādhi, gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and even explains it to others for a mere moment, they shall yet obtain an immeasurable and boundless accumulation of merit; how much more so for those sons or daughters of good family who, regarding this sūtra of the samādhi, believe as they have heard, accept as they have believed, explain as they have accepted, and practice as they have explained?
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"If one were to fill the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system with the seven treasures and practice *dāna* (generosity) thereby,
though I say that person's merit would be vast, it would not equal even a small portion of the merit gained from hearing this sutra."
If a bodhisattva, seeking a great mass of merit, has faith and understanding, recites and chants, further contemplates,
explains, practices, and maintains mindfulness of samādhi, the merit obtained thereby far exceeds that [of the former].
Suppose the entire trichiliocosm were ground into dust, and each particle of dust were further divided into as many parts as there were originally;
if one were to take all such particles of lands, fill them with precious jewels, and practice *dāna*;
yet if one were to explain even a single verse of this Samādhi Sūtra praised by all Buddhas to another person— [the merit of the latter would far exceed that of the former].
I say that such a person attains merit that surpasses the immeasurable blessings of ordinary giving.
If one further explains this fully to others, even for as brief a moment as it takes to milk a cow once,
contemplating and expanding these roots of goodness— how much more so for long-term, immeasurable blessings?
If all sentient beings were to become Buddhas, and with pure wisdom they were to ultimately realize that Suchness,
even if one were to recite this verse for many hundreds of millions of kalpas, the merit thereof could not be exhausted;
for even after those Buddhas have all passed into extinction, one might continue to proclaim it extensively for many hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Even in the end, one would not exhaust the limit of that merit gained from this profound sūtra’s four-line verse.

Suppose all the worlds that exist—in the four directions, above, below, and the four intermediate points—were filled with various jewels and offered to others, presented to the Buddhas in pursuit of supreme merit; [the merit of the former would still surpass it].
Those various merits are difficult to measure; if one were to calculate them, they would equal all the worlds.
Whoever hears and receives this samādhi and is well able to proclaim it, their merit shall exceed the former.
If a person has no doubt regarding this, they will also clearly understand all phenomena;
such a one shall forever sever the paths of evil rebirths and be able to enter the sublime, tranquil samādhi of dhyāna.
If they can constantly make offerings to me, they will surely receive inconceivable and manifold blessings;
their great learning will increase and they shall realize bodhi, by contemplating the meditative concentration praised by all Buddhas.
Now I speak these words of truth to you: You should be mindful and diligent, never being heedless;
With a single mind of joy, rouse your heroic vigor, And you shall naturally and swiftly realize that Bodhi.
Having made offerings to hundreds of Buddhas, he is now able to receive this samādhi;
even in a future age of terror, he shall personally and swiftly realize this subtle and wondrous concentration.
If there are those who see me together with the bhikṣus, as well as you, the Great Being Bhadrapāla and others—
such bodhisattvas who delight in extensive learning will certainly attain this samādhi.
If one hears this noble samādhi, explains it for others, or writes it down—
this dhāraṇī is praised by the World-Honored One— and one will be able to realize the bodhi of all Buddhas.
If a person skillfully contemplates this samādhi, all Buddhas will join in praising them;
they shall attain noble lineage and great learning, as the Buddhas explain in successive order.
Chapter Six: Observation. The Great Collection Sūtra, Section on Bhadrapāla, Chapter Six, Part One. At that time, the Blessed One again addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying: "Bhadrapāla!"
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to contemplate this samādhi, how should they contemplate it? Bhadrapāla!
Those bodhisattvas who wish to contemplate it should contemplate in this way:
"Just as our World-Honored One now dwells among the assembly of devas and humans proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma," so it was, O Bhadrapāla,

that the Bodhisattva thus single-mindedly contemplated all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas seated upon lion thrones proclaiming the True Dharma— endowed with the perfection of all marks and signs, most wondrous, most supreme, uniquely majestic and dignified, and such that one could gaze upon them without ever wearying.
"In this way, when observing the marks of a Great Man, one should apply the utmost sincerity to each individual mark; thus, one will clearly behold all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Having beheld them, one should first inquire about the mark of the invisible crown of the head (anavalokitamūrdhatā).
Once the inquiry has been made, one should thereafter observe all the marks in succession, causing each to be clearly perceived."
Having observed this, he further reflects: "The various marks of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are subtle and wondrous; they are truly rare.

May I, in the future, likewise attain such a body fully endowed with all these exquisite marks. May I, in the future, likewise attain such pure precepts and be fully endowed with majestic deportment. May I, in the future, likewise attain such fullness of samādhi. May I, in the future, likewise attain such fullness of wisdom. May I, in the future, likewise attain such fullness of liberation. May I, in the future, likewise attain such knowledge and vision of liberation. Having perfected such a body of marks in the future, may I immediately achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Once you have attained Buddhahood, you too shall likewise dwell amidst that assembly of devas and humans and fully proclaim such a sublime Dharma.
"Once the Bodhisattva has thus fully observed the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, and so forth, up until the accomplishment of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), he should further reflect in this way:
'Among these, what is "I"?'"
Who is it that possesses the dharmas of "mine"?
Who is able to attain the bodhi of all Buddhas?
Is it attained by means of the body?
Is it attained by the mind?

If it were attained by the body, this body is dull and insentient, devoid of sensation and cognition, like grass, wood, stone walls, or reflections in a mirror. Furthermore, that bodhi is without color and without form; it is neither an image nor a characteristic; it cannot be seen or known, nor can it be touched or realized. How, then, could one attain that bodhi with a body that is dull, insentient, without cognition, without vision, without consciousness, without discrimination, and without action?

Awakening is likewise: being without form or color, neither a characteristic nor an image, it cannot be seen or known, nor can it be touched or realized. Who, then, could practice or realize it within it?
If one seeks this mind, it is formless and cannot be seen;
it is signless and cannot be known.
This mind is thus, identical to an illusion.
Yet that bodhi is likewise: it is formless and invisible, signless and unknowable, untainted and unconditioned, and is also like an illusion.
"How can it be realized?
How can it be known so that one may say that body and mind attain bodhi?

When those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas contemplate in this way, they see with perfect clarity that these bodily characteristics do not attain bodhi, and they also know that this mind does not attain bodhi.
Why is this? Because among all phenomena, there is nothing by which form can be realized through form, nor by which mind can be realized through mind.

Nevertheless, within the realm of verbal expression, one knows that all phenomena, though they are without color, without form, without marks, and without outflows, are neither visible nor subject to realization, yet they are not without realization either.
Why is this? Because the bodies of all Tathāgatas are without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, because the bodies of all Tathāgatas are without outflows, their minds are also without outflows.
Furthermore, because the minds of all Tathāgatas are without outflows (*anāsrava*), their form (*rūpa*) is also without outflows.
*The Sūtra Asked by the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla*, Scroll II;
*The Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, Bhadrapāla Chapter, Scroll III.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of Central India during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Investigation, Part Two.

"Furthermore, because the form (*rūpa*) of all Tathāgatas is without outflows (*anāsrava*), their sensation (*vedanā*) is also without outflows; likewise, even their formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are without outflows."

Furthermore, the precepts of all Tathāgatas are also untainted (anāsrava); their samādhis and wisdom are also untainted; and even their liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation are also untainted.
In this way, even all Tathāgatas and all that has been spoken, is being spoken, or will be spoken by all Tathāgatas, as well as all dharmas—these are all untainted (anāsrava).
“Bhadrapāla! All such Buddha-dharmas as these can be realized by the wise, but the ignorant do not know them.
When one is able to contemplate in this manner, all dharmas are entirely unattainable.”
How is it that they cannot be apprehended?
It is because one cannot apprehend who could realize them.
How is it that even realization itself cannot be apprehended?
For what reason? Because even the realization itself cannot be apprehended.
Having performed this contemplation, he thus enters the samādhi of cessation, wherein he neither discriminates among phenomena nor fails to discriminate among phenomena.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are non-existent. "Bhadrapāla!
Noble Protector! It is as if, when fire has not yet arisen, someone were to say at that time:
"I shall first extinguish this fire today.
Noble Protector!
"What do you think?
Are the words of that person truthful or not?
Bhadrapāla replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:
"In this way, all phenomena have been ultimately unobtainable from the very beginning; how can you now make such a claim as:
'I am able to realize and know all phenomena, I am able to comprehend all phenomena, I am able to awaken to all phenomena, and I am able to deliver all sentient beings'?"
"In the midst of birth and death, this is not the correct statement. Why is that?
Because within that dharma-realm, there have fundamentally been no dharmas, nor any sentient beings."
Why do you say "crossing over"?
It is merely a crossing over by way of causes and conditions within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), O Bhadrapāla!
"What do you think?
Is what he has said true? Bhadrapāla replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"Therefore, those sons and daughters of good family who wish to accomplish unsurpassed bodhi, or even wish to accomplish the bodhi of a pratyekabuddha or the bodhi of a śrāvaka, should all contemplate all dharmas in this manner."
When one practices this contemplation, one enters into tranquil concentration, which is neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization.
Why is this? O Bhadrapāla!
All those phenomena are non-existent and unarisen.

Yet, the definite existence of conceptualization is one extreme, and the definite non-existence of conceptualization is another extreme. However, that which belongs to these two extremes is neither tranquil nor non-tranquil; it is a place without deliberation, a place without conceptualization, a place without realization, a place without activity, a place without accumulation, a place without recollection, and a place without origination.
Bhadrapāla!
This is called the Middle Way—because all numerical categories, locations, and so forth are spoken of merely in accordance with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"
Within that reality of the ultimate truth, neither the middle nor the extremes can be apprehended.
Why is this? O Bhadrapāla!

All phenomena are like space; they are quiescent from the very beginning, neither annihilated nor eternal, without accumulation, without a place of abiding, and without anything upon which to rely. They are signless, unconditioned, and beyond calculation.
Bhadrapāla!
That which is incalculable—how could it be said to exist?
Because it is incalculable, it does not enter into the realm of calculation.
Because they do not enter into numerical reckoning, there is ultimately no calculation, name, or designation for them. "Bhadrapāla!
When those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe the Tathāgatas in this manner, they must not cling to them."

Why is this? Because all phenomena are without attachment; since there is no locus to which one may attach, nor is there any root that can be severed, and because the root has been eliminated, there is no basis for dependence.

“Bhadrapāla! That bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate the samādhi of the manifestation of all buddhas before one’s eyes in this way: having thus seen all the Tathāgatas, one should not become attached to them, nor should one grasp hold of them.”
Why is this? Bhadrapāla!
All dharmas cannot be grasped or maintained; they are like space, their essential nature being quiescent extinction.

“Bhadrapāla! It is as if a golden hammer were placed within a fire; though the furnace and bellows are skillfully managed, it is melted, refined, and smelted until it becomes fiercely and intensely hot.
Or again, it is like an iron ball that has just emerged from the fire, blazing and glowing with intense heat; a person of wisdom should not grasp or touch it.”
Why is this? Because molten iron flows with blazing gold; anything that touches it is set ablaze.
Thus it is, Bhadrapāla!
A bodhisattva’s contemplation of the Buddha should not involve grasping or attachment; such is the nature of this matter.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva contemplates the form of the Buddha, they should not give rise to attachment;
likewise, when contemplating sensation, and so forth, up to volitional formations and consciousness, they should not give rise to attachment.
Furthermore, when that bodhisattva contemplates ethical discipline, he should not become attached to it;
likewise, when contemplating concentration, up to wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, he should not become attached to them either.
Why is this? For those who harbor attachment can never escape the phenomena of suffering within birth and death, as all such phenomena of suffering arise from attachment.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva contemplates these Tathāgatas in this manner, they should not give rise to thoughts of attachment.
“Bhadrapāla!

Although there is no grasping or attachment, one should nevertheless diligently seek the supreme and wondrous merits of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—namely, the Buddha-wisdom, the Tathāgata-wisdom, the vast wisdom, the self-arisen wisdom, the sovereign wisdom, the inconceivable wisdom, the immeasurable wisdom, the unequaled wisdom, and the wisdom of all-knowledge.”
"If you wish to seek entry into such wisdom, you should always diligently contemplate and observe the Samādhi of Seeing the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:

"Just as a bright mirror or an oil vessel, With a woman’s adorned form shining within, If one desires to see her beauty, One must gaze with focused attention; So too, if one wishes to see the Buddha, One must practice the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha."
The fool conceives a defiled mind therein, racing everywhere in pursuit of desire.
Regarding that which is non-existent, he harbors perverted perceptions; he does not know that these phenomena arise from delusion.
Consumed by the blazing fire of his lust, this woman gives rise to desire, which in turn flares up within him.
If there is a bodhisattva who forms this thought:
"This is called the mind of ignorant attachment; the nectar of enlightenment lies in the future, and I shall pull sentient beings out of their heavy suffering."
In the ultimate sense, there are no sentient beings; in this world, there is only birth, old age, and death.
All phenomena are formless like the moon reflected in water; how could there be any *bodhi* to be sought?
The various forms and appearances are like reflections in a mirror; They are like illusions, like mirages, like space.
Ordinary people cling to these perceptions and suffer bondage; Yet though they are bound, it is empty and lacks reality.
If such wise Bodhisattvas, knowing the world’s perversion, perceive the truth;
and thoroughly understanding that there is no person, they see that none undergoes suffering—they shall then attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
Without conceptualizing the Buddha’s bodhi, his mind is fundamentally and originally luminous and pure;
seeing neither birth nor death nor any defilements, he realizes the truth as the most supreme Honored One.
All form-phenomena and all outflows are beyond conceptual differentiation, being illusory and empty;
by extinguishing all desires and liberating the mind, one who knows thus realizes samādhi.
First, one contemplates the signless body of all Buddhas; Later, one hears that all dharmas are fundamentally pure.
If one reflects thus without any other thoughts, Realizing this samādhi will truly not be difficult.
Constantly contemplating the mark of emptiness, one is able to extinguish that accumulation of atoms;
by not discriminating between formation and destruction, all non-Buddhists lose their way therein.
Making no conceptual distinctions regarding any forms, though their eyes behold them, these do not burden the mind;
they see all Buddhas like the orb of the sun, transcending both the dharma-realm and the world.
Their minds are pure and their eyes are clear; though they exert themselves with diligence, they always abide in meditative concentration.
Their attainment of great learning is ineffable, as they realize this samādhi through true contemplation.
If one were to realize samādhi through non-seeing, then all who are blind should likewise realize it;
yet it is realized neither by seeing nor by not seeing—within this, all those of external paths are utterly deluded.
Constantly contemplating while remaining free from the perception of signs, One beholds the pure minds of those Buddhas;
Having seen them thus through all observations, That person will swiftly accomplish this samādhi.
He has no earth, water, fire, or wind, nor does he abide manifest within the realm of space;
yet if one wishes to observe all Buddhas, one should imagine him seated upon his throne, proclaiming the wondrous sound of the Dharma.
As I proclaim the sublime Dharma today, those whose hearts delight in the Dharma who behold my body should no longer harbor any other thoughts;
they should contemplate only the Buddha’s act of teaching the Dharma.
Thus, focus your attention exclusively and do not look elsewhere;
for the sake of seeking such great learning, contemplate with a single mind this samādhi that I have taught, which is the dhāraṇī proclaimed by all Buddhas.
There is not a single Buddha who existed in the past, nor any in the present or the future;
there is only this pure and subtle dhyāna, which cannot be described even by one who has realized it.
I, the Unsurpassed Honored One within the three realms, have appeared specifically for the sake of benefiting the world;
mindful of realizing the Bodhi of all Buddhas, I proclaim this peerless samādhi.
If you desire physical and mental bliss, seek the inconceivable merit of the Buddhas,
and even attain that wondrous Bodhi, you must practice this supreme samādhi.
Desiring to purify the vast and deep ocean of extensive learning, one should always seek it with diligence for the sake of sentient beings;
such a person should swiftly remove the dust of all desires and must practice this supreme samādhi.

If you wish to see many Buddhas in a single lifetime, and having seen them, pay them homage and inquire further, you should quickly abandon [worldly things] and not give rise to attachment; you must certainly contemplate this wondrous samādhi.
In this place there is neither desire nor hatred, Nor is there folly, delusion, or envy;
Furthermore, there is no ignorance or the net of doubt— One must dwell here in this profound and tranquil meditation.

Chapter Seven: Perfection of Ethical Conduct. In the *Bhadrapāla-parivarta* of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, Chapter Seven: Perfection of Ethical Conduct. At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous, World-Honored One!”
Indeed, there is such a supreme samādhi as this.
World-Honored One!

If there are bodhisattvas who have left home for the homeless life and, with a profound mind, desire to expound this samādhi and also wish to contemplate it, in what dharma should they abide in order to be able to proclaim and contemplate it?
The Buddha said to Bhadrapāla: “Bhadrapāla!

If there is a bodhisattva who has left home to renounce the world, who deeply delights in widely proclaiming [the Dharma], and further wishes to contemplate such a samādhi, that renunciant bodhisattva should first protect and maintain pure conduct: conduct that is unimpaired, unstained, undefiled, unturbid, unattached, immovable, irreproachable, praised by the wise, and cherished by the noble ones; he should mindfully understand these various forms of precept.”
"Bhadrapāla! How should that renunciant bodhisattva attain pure conduct of the precepts, and even how should he attain the conduct of the precepts beloved and honored by the noble ones?"
Bhadrapāla!

That renunciant bodhisattva should rely upon that prātimokṣa to perfect their deportment and perfect all practices, even down to the precepts as numerous as atoms; having seen them, they should be struck with awe and fear, and maintain a pure livelihood.

Among all the precepts, one should contemplate their fulfillment and maintain faith in their profound depth; one must not become attached to forbearance, and when hearing the teachings on emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the mind shall not be startled or terrified, nor shall it fall into regret or despondency.
Bhadrapāla!

By these causes and conditions, that renunciant bodhisattva accomplishes such pure conduct of the precepts—neither perceiving the conduct of the precepts nor clinging to the conduct of the precepts, even unto the accomplishment of the conduct of the precepts cherished and revered by the noble ones.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How can those bodhisattvas who have left the household life come to possess such impure conduct regarding the precepts, deficient conduct regarding the precepts, defiled conduct regarding the precepts, sullied conduct regarding the precepts, dependent conduct regarding the precepts, conduct regarding the precepts censured by the wise, and conduct regarding the precepts not cherished by the noble ones?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying:
"Bhadrapāla! If there is an ordained bodhisattva who grasps at form, upholds the prohibitive precepts, and practices the holy life;
In this way, clinging to feeling, clinging to perception, clinging to formations, and clinging to consciousness, one upholds the prohibitive precepts and practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Having practiced it, one forms this thought:

"By my thus maintaining the precepts, thus practicing asceticism, thus training, and thus practicing the holy life, may I in the future be born in the heavens or among humans, possessing autonomous existence and receiving various karmic fruits."

"Bhadrapāla! For these reasons, that renunciant bodhisattva accomplishes such impure precepts, even precepts not cherished by the noble ones; this is said to be for the sake of seeking existence, for the sake of the arising of birth, for the sake of receiving the fruits of desire, and for the sake of taking up a place of rebirth."

“Bhadrapāla! Therefore, a renunciant bodhisattva who intends to speak of this samādhi or contemplate this samādhi must first be fully endowed with pure conduct of the precepts, up to and including the accomplishment of the precepts cherished by the noble ones; furthermore, he must also keep them in mind.”
He constantly practices the perfection of giving— namely, the most excellent gift, the gift of all dharmas, the supreme gift, the wondrous gift,
the sublime gift, the exquisite gift, and the unsurpassed gift— and he is also always courageous and diligent,
never resting, never casting off his heavy burden, never forgetting right mindfulness, and always practicing with single-minded concentration.
With right faith and purity, free from envy, and unattached to worldly gain or fame, one seeks only what is in accordance with the Dharma to sustain life;
one constantly practices alms-gathering and does not accept special invitations;
one feels weary of and detached from human society, delights in *āraṇya* (forest hermitages), honors the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), reveres the ascetic practices (*dhūta*), and brings rest to...
Regarding worldly speech, one should discuss only that which transcends the world; when among the multitude, one remains silent and uses few words.
One always respects others and does not dare to treat them with contempt; at all times, one constantly practices a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*).

One recognizes kindness received and surely repays it; one constantly keeps in mind the need to draw near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and treats all teachers and venerable ones with the utmost care.
There shall be no contradiction to this matter.

If one hears such a profound sutra as this, listens and receives it with single-minded devotion without ever becoming weary, and conceives toward the Dharma Master a mind of a compassionate father and a mind of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), even generating the perception of him as a Tathāgata—for the sake of such a subtle and wondrous Dharma, for the sake of accomplishing unsurpassed Great Bodhi, and because of the ever-increasing heart of love, reverence, and respect—[one shall attain the aforementioned fruits].
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

If a bodhisattva should at any time go to the place of a śrāvaka and hear such a profound sūtra-dharma, yet lacks a heart of love and respect for that Dharma-preacher, lacks a heart of reverence, does not conceive of him as a compassionate father, does not conceive of him as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), does not conceive of him as a Buddha, and does not conceive of him as a teacher; if he is unable to draw near, serve, and make offerings to him—then wherever he may hear this sūtra, you should know that this person is incapable of hearing and receiving it, copying it, explaining it, or causing the Dharma to endure for a long time.
For such a person to be able to hear and receive it, to copy it, to explain it, or to cause the Dharma to endure for a long time—that is impossible."
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

If that bodhisattva, having gone to the place of a śrāvaka, hears such a sublime and superior Dharma being taught, yet does not give rise to a mind of love and reverence, does not give rise to a mind of respect, and even does not conceive the thought of them as Buddhas, and is unable to approach and make offerings to them with all his heart—then it is impossible for him to be able to read and recite it, to receive and uphold it, or to explain it so as to prevent this sūtra from quickly disappearing."
Why is this? Because they do not respect this sutra, this Dharma will surely perish before long.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

If that bodhisattva, or perhaps having gone to the place of a śrāvaka, hears such a subtle and wondrous sūtra as this, and gives rise to a heart of love and respect, a heart of reverence, and conceives of them as a teacher and as all the Tathāgatas, personally attending to and making offerings to them, then he will be able to hear and receive it, as well as write it down, explain it, and cause this sūtra to endure for a long time for the benefit of others—this is indeed possible.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

If that bodhisattva, having heard such a subtle and wondrous sūtra from a śrāvaka, should give rise toward him a mind of respect, regarding him as if he were a Buddha, and should attend upon, serve, honor, and make offerings to him—such a person, though not yet having studied this sūtra, is as one who has practiced it; though not yet having explained it, is as one who has expounded it. It is possible that they will cause this sublime Dharma to abide long in the world, neither being defiled nor extinguished."
Why is this? Because they are able to love, revere, and honor the Dharma, this sutra will abide long in the world. "Bhadrapāla!

For these reasons, I now tell you: toward this Dharma-preacher, such a person gives rise to a heart of love and joy, a heart of reverence, and a heart of esteem; they conceive of him as a spiritual friend, as a teacher, and as a Buddha, serving him with all their heart and honoring him with offerings.
"Bhadrapāla!
If one can act in this way, they are said to be practicing what I practice and receiving my instructions.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

A renunciant bodhisattva who wishes to explain this samādhi and further desires to contemplate it should always delight in practicing the affairs of an araṇya; they must not dwell in villages or towns,
but should abandon places of social cliques and excessive seeking, and must not covet food or clothing nor hoard them.
One must not accept or store wealth, provisions, or material resources; one must not greedily seek fame or gain.
One should disregard even one’s own life, constantly mindful of sacrificing the body; remaining far removed from greedy attachment, one should perpetually cultivate the contemplation of death.
Always practicing shame and remorse, one should commit no evil and embrace the True Dharma without doubt.

The mind should always be mindful of detachment and refrain from grasping at various signs; one should cultivate a heart of loving-kindness and harbor no resentment, constantly giving rise to compassion and mercy while refraining from anger;
one should settle the mind in joy and equanimity, harboring no thoughts of love or hatred, and should always practice walking meditation to dispel the hindrance of drowsiness.
Bhadrapāla!
If a renunciant bodhisattva can abide securely in such Dharma practice, they will be able to cultivate, explain, and contemplate this Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!
The sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha are most profound and deep, most supreme and subtle, and inconceivable."

However, those bodhisattvas of the future who are indolent and lazy, although they hear such profound and wondrous sūtras, will give rise to great terror, alarm, and doubt, and will retreat and sink back, failing to develop a heart of joy and delight.
They will further think thus:
"I must now go to the presence of other Buddhas in order to practice such sutras as these. Why is this?"

"I now know for myself that there are many obstacles and difficulties; my body is afflicted by the suffering of illness and my strength is extremely slight. How could I possibly be capable of practicing such a sutra as this?
"World-Honored One! [he continued.]
Such as they are, they will develop a mind of further indifference and detachment toward the profound Dharma, unable to exert diligent and heroic effort, nor desiring to accomplish such a sutra.
“World-Honored One!
At that time, there will also be bodhisattvas who diligently seek with vigor and single-minded mindfulness, who delight in this Dharma, exhort others to uphold this Dharma, and embrace this Dharma.”

If there are Dharma masters who preach this Dharma, because they practice in accordance with the Dharma within this teaching, they are able to relinquish body and life; they do not crave fame, do not seek gain and offerings, do not proclaim their own virtues, do not become attached to robes and bowls, and do not delight in cities and towns, but always resort to empty, secluded places in mountains and forests.

Should they, upon hearing this subtle and wondrous Dharma, give rise to great joy, they shall further fully develop diligent vigor to hear and receive such a subtle Dharma-gate; by constantly reading and reciting it, constantly contemplating and upholding it, reflecting upon its meaning, and practicing according to the teaching, they will, in future lives before all Tathāgatas, not merely seek extensive learning nor simply seek to abide in existence, but solely for the sake of accomplishing all merits, they will constantly and diligently seek with vigor and courage.
“World-Honored One!

Furthermore, there must be sons and daughters of good family who have previously made offerings to various Buddhas and planted roots of goodness in the past, who give rise to great diligence for the sake of hearing such a subtle and wondrous Dharma.

They further make such a solemn vow of adornment: ‘I vow that even if my skin becomes parched, my bones scatter, and my marrow wastes away; even if my body and mind burn with fervor and I practice asceticism without ceasing—I must achieve this sublime scripture. I shall never for a moment be indolent or lazy and fail to listen to this subtle and supreme Dharma; nor shall I fail to contemplate its profound principles; nor shall I abandon others and fail to proclaim it for them. Rather, I shall always practice great diligence with valor, solely for the sake of gathering in all Bodhisattvas, to hear such a sublime scripture from the Tathāgata.’”
Having heard this, he immediately gave rise to a heart of joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
Bhadrapāla!
It is so, it is so, just as you have said; I now rejoice in this.
Bhadrapāla!
“Because I rejoice in this, all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the three periods of time, likewise rejoice.
Then, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If there is a lay bodhisattva dwelling in the world who hears of this samādhi and wishes to contemplate it for himself and then explain it to others—even for a single day or a single night—how many kinds of practices must such a person abide in to achieve the contemplation of this samādhi and be able to explain it to others?”
The Buddha said:
“Bhadrapāla! When that lay bodhisattva dwells in the world, if he wishes to practice and contemplate samādhi—”
"—whether for a day, a night, or even as long as it takes to milk a cow—listen now to what I say to you:
that householder bodhisattva, dwelling in the world, should maintain right faith and not give rise to stinginess or greed;
he should constantly mindfully practice giving, giving according to whatever he has, whether much or little, and should practice universal giving."
Seeking the fruit of retribution, one should take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and likewise take refuge in the Saṅgha;
one should not serve celestial deities, nor perform prostrations to them; one should not give rise to envy, but always maintain sympathetic joy;
one must live a pure life in accordance with the Dharma, without craving for children, without attachment to a wife or concubines, and without being defiled by [sensual desires].

While living at home, they do not crave wealth or treasures; they always delight in leaving the household life, constantly mindful of shaving their hair and beards, practicing the eightfold precepts, and dwelling perpetually in monasteries.
They always maintain a sense of shame and remorse, resolve upon bodhicitta, and do not think of other vehicles.
Upon seeing bhikṣus who uphold the precepts with purity and practice the Brahma-faring life, they never engage in frivolous jesting.
One should always practice reverence.

From whomever one hears and studies this samādhi, one should give rise to a heart of love and respect toward that teacher, conceive a sense of veneration, regard them as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), perceive them as a preceptor, and conceive of them as a Buddha. One should offer all requisites to them, always acknowledging their kindness and constantly reflecting on how to repay their virtue, because they have been able to teach one the subtle and wondrous Dharma.

“Bhadrapāla! When that lay bodhisattva dwells in the secular world, having established himself in such practices of all dharmas, he should thereafter instruct [others] in this samādhi, this reflection, and this cultivation.”
Then the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!

It is now that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of those bodhisattvas—both monastic and lay—who have accomplished right faith and delight in the profound Dharma, proclaims such unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma, causing them to abide in such immeasurable practices of the Dharma, and only thereafter shall they be able to contemplate and explain this samādhi."
“World-Honored One!
After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, will this samādhi be able to be widely practiced in Jambudvīpa?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying:
“Bhadrapāla! After my parinirvāṇa, this Samādhi Sūtra shall circulate widely throughout Jambudvīpa for forty years;
thereafter, during the final five hundred years—the hundredth year when the True Dharma is perishing—”
When I, Kāśyapa, practice evil; when the true Dharma is slandered; when the true Dharma is being destroyed; when the observance of precepts declines;

when the breaking of precepts flourishes; and when various nations wage war against one another—at such times as these, there will be sentient beings whose roots of goodness are blazing, who have already in the past drawn near to various Buddhas and made offerings to them.
Through their practice and planting of seeds of goodness, for the sake of those noble sons so that they may obtain this sutra,
this scripture of samādhi shall once again circulate in Jambudvīpa; it is by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha that,
after my parinirvāṇa, they shall hear this sutra and joyfully transcribe, read, and recite it.
“...uphold it, contemplate its meaning, explain it to others, and practice according to its teaching.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla and the Licchavi Ratnākara, hearing the Tathāgata speak of the time when the True Dharma would perish, wept with tears falling like rain. They rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years—the last century—when śramaṇas have become perverted, when the True Dharma is about to perish, when the True Dharma is being slandered, when the True Dharma is being destroyed, when the observance of precepts declines, when the breaking of precepts increases, when the protection of the True Dharma diminishes, when the protection of what is not the Dharma increases, when sentient beings are in turmoil, and when various nations wage war against one another—we shall be able to read, recite, receive and uphold, contemplate the meaning of, and extensively explain for others the sublime samādhis within the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because my mind knows no weariness and never attains contentment.

Therefore, regarding the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, I am able to hear them, write them down, read and recite them, receive and uphold them, contemplate them, practice them, and explain them extensively.

At that time, the merchant leader, the lay follower (upāsaka) Gaṅgottara, son of a householder, the young brahmin (māṇava) Naradatta, and others, having heard the Tathāgata speak of the destruction of the True Dharma in future ages, wept with sorrow for the sake of the True Dharma. They rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We shall protect and sustain both the sublime sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata and those who uphold these sūtras, causing them all to flourish and increase.
World-Honored One!
I shall now further provide my protective empowerment for the subtle and wondrous sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, so that they may be widely proclaimed and long endure in the world. Why is this?
Because this sutra can bring about the accomplishment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for many beings throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]
"We have heard this unprecedented Dharma; we shall receive and uphold it with a sincere heart, contemplate its meaning, explain it to others, and widely propagate it.
World-Honored One!"

Having now heard this profound Dharma of the sutra, there is no one in all the worlds who would believe it; therefore, I shall first create for them the vessel of roots of goodness, and only then provide the explanation.

At that time, among the assembly were five hundred bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—these four groups—who, upon hearing the Tathāgata speak of the destruction and extinction of the True Dharma in future ages, wept with tears like rain out of grief for the sake of the True Dharma. They rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We shall uphold the True Dharma of the Tathāgata; however, at that time, may those Great Beings and virtuous men act as our true reliance, provide us with protection, and manage affairs for us, so that we may grasp the true meaning within such profound sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata and practice in accordance with the Dharma.
We only pray, World-Honored One,
that you entrust us, these good men, and establish a clear record for us. Why is this?
“World-Honored One!
I and they are all able to protect, uphold, and embrace the True Dharma, as well as those who embrace it.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled and emitted golden light. This radiance shone throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, then returned to the presence of the Buddha, circled him three times to the right, and vanished into the crown of his head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has smiled many times since the past; however, whenever he smiles, it is invariably for some extraordinary reason. I should now inquire about the cause and conditions of this smile."

Having reflected thus, he immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, addressed him in verse:
“Your mind is pure and your conduct is untainted; You possess great majesty and vast supernormal powers.
Most honored among all, supreme in the world, You appear stainless like the bright moon.”
With unimpeded noble wisdom and a liberated mind, possessing the kalaviṅka-like voice supreme among gods, you cannot be moved by any heterodox arguments; for what reason do you now suddenly smile?
Thoroughly penetrating the true and correct, speak for our sake; O Honored One among Two-legged Beings, you are able to bring great benefit.
Hearing this subtle and wondrous voice of the Tathāgata, all shall be filled with great joy.
How could the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, smile in vain?
The Buddha has again emitted light; there must be a superior person present.
Who, on this day, has attained great benefit?
Therefore, you should now proclaim the meaning of your smile:
who today has attained realization of the Truth?
Who today has received the Dharma-kingdom?
Who today receives self-consecration?
Who today ascends to the rank of Buddha?
Who today benefits the world?
Who shall fully proclaim the treasury of the Buddha's Dharma?
Who shall attain eternal abiding in the Buddha's wisdom?
For these reasons, O Honored One, you should reveal the cause of your smile.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Ānanda with these verses: “Ānanda!
Do you see this great assembly?”
Fifty hundred [disciples] rose from their seats, their bodies and minds filled with joy, and uttered these sincere words:
"In the future, we shall obtain this Dharma.
With single-minded devotion, they gazed upon me.
"When shall we ourselves likewise become so?
they all made this great vow before me:
"We shall realize this path in the future."
Furthermore, there will be eight classes who rise from their seats, with five hundred leaders as their foremost;
in the final age when the Dharma is decaying, they shall proclaim it for the sake of the world's teachings.
I now tell you these words: among this assembly, those who possess unimpeded wisdom have not, at the station of a single Buddha, risen and joined their palms in reverence to the Honored Ones.
I contemplate the immeasurable past eons, when eighty thousand Buddhas appeared before me;
eight people, led by these eight, rose from their seats and likewise upheld this wondrous Dharma.
Prior to this, eighty trillion *yojanas* ago, they again encountered Buddhas in such numbers;
having attained liberation of mind and great renown, these individuals already upheld [the teachings] at that time.
Now, furthermore, within my supreme Dharma, you are able to act as the foremost in providing protection and benefit;
you shall teach and transform immeasurable multitudes of bodhisattvas and eliminate envy among all great beings.
When I have entered parinirvāṇa, these ones shall take my relics and offer worship;
skillfully upholding these various Buddha-deeds of mine, they shall place them within caskets throughout the ten directions.
Whether building stupas on level ground or upon mountains, they shall entrust them to devas, nāgas, and garuḍas.
Relying upon this sūtra, these beings shall all be reborn in the heavens at the end of their lives;
though they later take birth again in the human realm, they shall never be separated from noble lineages.
Skillfully upholding these matters of my bodhi, they shall again give rise to great vows in accordance with their original resolve.
Sometimes, for the sake of the Dharma, he travels to other lands, where he constantly encounters such profound and wondrous scriptures;
having obtained them, he transmits them to many people with a joyful heart, free from envy.
Seeking the Dharma with such sincerity that one never tires; regarding wealth as light and life as cheap, how could one cherish the self?
Subduing all external doctrines, one constantly bestows the wondrous Dharma upon others as a gift.
At that time, there was no one in the world capable of receiving this sutra, nor anyone to read, recite, or transmit its teachings;
there were only these five hundred worthy ones who have now risen from their seats before me.
Furthermore, these eight bodhisattvas shall, in the future, receive this Dharma in the northern heavens;
delighting in its constant and widespread proclamation for the great benefit of others, they shall propagate this profound sūtra.
These eight upright men shall be the leaders; their number shall remain exactly five hundred, neither more nor less.
Free from envy and having cast aside fame, they shall in a future age receive the transmission of the vast Dharma.
Such bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as upāsakas and upāsikās,
who possess skillful wisdom, are free from envy, and ascend to the rank of Dharma masters, shall attain perfect enlightenment with great majestic power.
He is endowed with inconceivable divine virtues, his body adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings;
having attained subtle and wondrous bliss, he eliminates all suffering and forever uproots the afflictions of the three poisons.
From this day forth, after they have cast off their lives, they shall never again be born within the evil realms;
in all their births, they shall always remain in harmony, encountering only the most supreme matters of enlightenment.
Having already abandoned rebirth in all evil destinies, And being able to forever leave behind all states of hardship, The limits of their merit cannot be known;
Thus they receive immeasurable and manifold blessings.
Furthermore, one shall behold Maitreya Buddha, Constantly giving rise to a mind of harmony toward him;
Respectfully making offerings and benefiting others, Solely for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, these people will constantly assemble together to serve the World-Transcending Honored One among bipeds;
for the sake of this wondrous Bodhi of all Buddhas, they shall cross over birth and death and ascend to the other shore.
In the future final age when the Dharma is decaying, they too shall constantly uphold this teaching;
dwelling thus, they will always practice, and their affairs will be like those of the time of Maitreya.
Throughout this entire Bhadrakalpa, wherever they act as lamps for the world to bring vast benefit,
may they protect this sutra in all those places, dwelling with fearlessness throughout the three periods of time.
In the future, there will be many Buddhas numbering in the hundreds of millions, inconceivable and beyond measure;
they shall all make extensive offerings and practice widely, always protecting such supreme Buddha-deeds as these.
Those who have previously attained enlightenment, each of whom practiced and made offerings together with me,
may have already entered parinirvāṇa long ago, while I have remained for many nayutas of eons.
Now this Great Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, along with Ratnākara and the eminent treasures,
the merchant leader Mukta and Gamana, shall behold countless Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
There too he received this unsurpassed sutra; though many kalpas have already passed, no subtle calculation can exhaust its form—who could know its measure across immeasurable billions of kalpas?
If there are sentient beings who hear this name, whether during their waking hours or in their dreams,
and are able to let out the courageous lion’s roar, they shall all become honored among gods and humans.
If there are sentient beings who merely hear the name, And are able to believe, revere, and rejoice in it, They will all become Buddhas without any doubt;
How much more so for those who make offerings to his person?
The Dharma he has received is inconceivable; his lifespan and his abiding in the Dharma are likewise immeasurable.
His benefit is vast and inexhaustible; his merit and wisdom cannot be fathomed.
Those past Buddhas were inconceivable in number, as pure in their observance of the precepts as the sands of the Ganges;
these beings practiced extensive giving before them, seeking only the unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment.
Those various merits are beyond counting; though proclaimed for many eons, they could never be exhausted.
Within the state of Bodhi, there is neither increase nor decrease; one should always mindfully protect and uphold this Dharma of the sutra.

Ānanda! If there are those who protect this sutra—whether by copying it, reciting it, or keeping it in mind—you should certainly arouse love and respect for them; they shall never be separated from these five hundred [disciples].

Ānanda! If a person upholds this sutra, they shall naturally strive with a diligent mind to seek steadfastness; by purely maintaining the prohibitive precepts and abandoning sleep, they will certainly attain this wondrous samādhi.

In my Vinaya, I have taught the Prātimokṣa; if bhikṣus train while dwelling in an araṇya, and if they can practice dhūta austerities without abandoning them, they will attain this samādhi without doubt.
One who can relinquish all private invitations and renounce every kind of fine delicacy,
and who constantly gives rise to the Buddha-mind toward their teacher— who could say that such a person has not realized this samādhi?
First perceiving the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, one completely abandons pride and envy;
with a mind free from defilement and attachment, one contemplates the unconditioned while reciting and reflecting upon the supreme samādhi.
The sphere of the mind is pure and free from defilement; the senses are subdued and resentment is stilled.
With single-minded devotion, one contemplates the body of the Tathāgata, reciting and upholding this wondrous samādhi.
If there is a bodhisattva living as a householder, whose mind always remains firmly established in the affairs of renunciation,
who accomplishes the vocal karma by upholding, receiving, reading, and reciting [the teachings], and whose mind constantly remembers to train in this samādhi.
One should always practice the five precepts, And constantly observe the eightfold fast;
Dwelling permanently in temples and relinquishing worldly possessions, One should recite and contemplate this samādhi.
One should not be attached to many wives and concubines, nor should one love children, grandchildren, or precious wealth;
abiding in the conduct of a lay follower with shame and modesty, one should simply remember and uphold this samādhi.
Do not give rise to thoughts of malice toward others; think only of eliminating all frivolity.
Without any place for attachment, abide in patience, and simply contemplate this samādhi.

Do not give rise to attachment toward wealth and goods; regarding flowers, perfumes, ointments, and various garlands, remain free from defiled attachment by abiding in patience, and simply uphold this samādhi.
If a bhikṣuṇī seeks this sūtra, she should diligently take refuge and pay homage while eliminating jealousy, frivolity, arrogance, and egoism;
for her, the realization of that bodhi will not be difficult.
One should arouse diligence to overcome sleep, severing all seeking;
with a mind that delights in the Dharma and maintains a pure livelihood, one should solely recite this samādhi.
The mind should never be associated with desire; do not give rise to anger or resentment, nor harbor any affliction.
Do not bind sentient beings with the fetters of Māra; you should only uphold this samādhi.
Do not act with flattery or crookedness; do not covet fine garments, ointments, or incense;
do not practice double-tongued speech to cause division among others; you should only uphold this samādhi.

Without being bound by thoughts of men or women, or sounds and forms, Tranquil and severed from all matters of perverse thought, One should conceive the notion of a Buddha toward the Teacher; One should solely uphold this samādhi.
Those born shall forever leave behind all evil realms; their faith in the Buddha-dharma shall not be in vain.
Having shattered all obstacles and difficulties within the three realms of existence, they must surely receive this samādhi.
The Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, Scroll Three;
The Bhadrapāla Section of the Mahāsaṃnipāta Mahāyāna Sūtra, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.

Chapter Eight: Praise of Meritorious Qualities At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Licchavi Ratnākara, the elder Śreṣṭhidāraka Gaṅgottara, the Māṇava Naradatta, the elder Varuṇa, and their retinues of five hundred followers, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly delighted. They immediately offered five hundred superior garments to cover the World-Honored One and further made offerings to the World-Honored One with various kinds of requisites. Because their hearts delighted in the Dharma, each of them personally attended upon the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"This Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla shall act as the teacher of the Dharma for those five hundred followers, expounding the essentials of all dharmas, instructing and consoling them, so as to cause them to rejoice."

Because of this joy, those people immediately attain a compliant mind, a true mind, a pure mind, and a mind free from desire; they eliminate all afflictions and are no longer bound by hindrances or entanglements.
Then those five hundred people, with single-minded devotion, joined their palms, paid homage with veneration, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“By being endowed with how many dharmas can a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain this buddhānusmṛti-samādhi?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Bhadrapāla, saying: “Bhadrapāla!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with four dharmas, they will attain this samādhi.
What are these four?

First, not being attached to the speech of any non-Buddhists; second, not delighting in any matters of sensual desire; third, never being separated from the merits of the dhūta practices; and fourth, always feeling weary of all places of birth within the three realms.
"Bhadrapāla!
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills them and attains this samādhi.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

If there are good sons or good daughters who read, recite, accept, and uphold this sūtra of samādhi, or who are further able to explain it for others, they shall immediately obtain five kinds of merit in the present life.

What are the five? First, no poisons whatsoever can cause harm; second, no weapons whatsoever can wound or injure; third, no waters whatsoever can drown or sweep away; fourth, no fierce fires whatsoever can burn; fifth, wicked kings and local officials cannot find an opportunity to seize them.
Why is this? It is because of the power of the mind of loving-kindness from this samādhi. "Bhadrapāla!

If those good sons or good daughters, when single-mindedly and diligently seeking this samādhi, reading and reciting it, receiving and upholding it, contemplating and practicing it, or explaining it for others, should encounter various poisons, weapons, water, fire, evil kings, or government officials who could cause them harm—such a thing is impossible.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

Suppose the fires of the kalpa of destruction were to arise, and the world were to blaze and the heavens and earth were to be set ablaze; if those sons of good family or daughters of good family who uphold this sūtra of samādhi should happen to fall into those great kalpa-fires, by the majestic power of the samādhi, those fires would immediately be extinguished."
Bhadrapāla!
Just as water in a jar can extinguish a small fire;
so it is, Bhadrapāla!

Even if those sons or daughters of good family who uphold this sutra should fall into that fire, by the power of their samādhi, the great fire will be extinguished accordingly; it is impossible that it would not be extinguished.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

If those sons or daughters of good family uphold this sutra, it is impossible that they should be harmed by an evil king, an evil official, bandits, lions, tigers, wolves, or venomous snakes—indeed, there is no such possibility for anyone who would create obstacles."

Furthermore, even if they should encounter obstacles while practicing this sutra—whether from yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, or any other non-human beings—it is impossible for such things to occur.

Furthermore, if those men or women are reciting the sutras, correctly contemplating them, explaining them to others, entering into samādhi, or practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), it is impossible for them to lose their robes or their alms bowls, or even to encounter any other obstructing circumstances—except in cases where past karmic retribution is so fixed that it cannot be averted.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

If those sons or daughters of good family who uphold this samādhi sūtra should suffer from ailments of the eyes, or ailments of the ears, or ailments of the nose, or ailments of the tongue, or ailments of the body, or ailments of the mind, or should encounter any other various kinds of calamities—even life-threatening dangers or obstacles to the holy life—such things shall not occur."
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

If those men or women have heard this sutra in such a way, seen it in such a way, known it in such a way, and become fully endowed with it, it is impossible that they would fail to meet a Buddha, slander the True Dharma, break the harmony of the Sangha, or turn their backs on the Bodhi of the Buddha."

Bhadrapāla, you should know that for those men and women who uphold this sūtra, none of the aforementioned matters shall be able to create obstacles—except for the consequences of past misdeeds, which cannot be averted.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
Those sons and daughters of good family who uphold this sutra shall always be praised by all the devas,
praised by all the nāgas, and also praised by all the yakṣas."
Furthermore, he is praised by all the gandharvas; he is praised by all the asuras; he is praised by all the garuḍas;
he is praised by all the kiṃnaras; and he is praised by all the mahoragas.
They are praised by all humans and non-humans;
they are praised by all the Four Great Heavenly Kings;
they are praised by all the Śakra-devānām-indras; and they are praised by all the Mahābrahmā-devaputras.
In this way, they shall even be constantly praised by all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
Moreover, those sons and daughters of good family who uphold this sutra shall always be loved and respected by all the devas."
In this way, they are constantly loved and respected by all dragons, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans;
furthermore, they are loved and respected by all the Four Great Heavenly Kings;
likewise, they are constantly loved and respected by all the Śakras, the kings of the gods, up to all the Mahābrahmā kings.
In this way, he is always cherished and remembered by all bodhisattvas, and even by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
Furthermore, by the power of this sutra, those sons and daughters of good family shall always be protected by all the devas;
likewise, they shall always be protected by all the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and humans and non-humans;
and they shall also be protected by all the Four Great Kings, as well as by the Trāyastriṃśa King up to the Great Brahmā King.

In this way, for the sake of all bodhisattvas, and even for all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, you shall provide protection for those who currently uphold the Dharma throughout the immeasurable, incalculable worlds of the ten directions.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
Moreover, by the power of this sutra, all the devas desire to see those good sons and good daughters;
likewise, all the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, as well as humans and non-humans, all think of desiring to see them."
Furthermore, all the Great Kings of the Four Heavenly Kings, as well as all the Kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven up to all the Great Brahmā Kings, all desire to see him;
likewise, all the bodhisattvas up to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, each desire to see him.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
Moreover, by the power of this sutra, all devas will constantly come to the place of those good sons and good daughters to personally manifest their forms for them to behold.
Likewise, all nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth, shall all see their forms and provide benefit according to what is appropriate."
Furthermore, all the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and even all the Great Brahmā Heavenly Kings personally come to behold them;

likewise, all the bodhisattvas and even all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—not only during the day but even within dreams—manifest their forms, proclaim their own names, touch their heads in blessing, offer consolation, and praise them to inspire and encourage them.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

Moreover, although those sons and daughters of good family have never heard other sūtras, by the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi, people will naturally come to their place—even in their dreams—to proclaim it for them, enabling them to hear it and to remember and uphold it without loss."
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

If I were to describe the merit obtained by those sons and daughters of good family who merely hold this subtle and wondrous sūtra of samādhi for a brief moment, even if it were to last for the duration of kalpas, I could never finish; though my wisdom and eloquence are inexhaustible, I could not fully express it—how much more so for those who hear this samādhi, practice according to the teaching, and abide in accordance with the Dharma?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses: "If there were one who could explain this,
The Great Quiescent and Supreme Samādhi of all Buddhas,
Even if I were now to describe its merit, It would be like taking a single grain of sand from the Ganges."
If one can expound this samādhi for others, water cannot drown them, fire cannot burn them, and they shall not be harmed by blades, staves, or poisons;
kings, thieves, and corrupt officials shall find no opportunity against them.
If one can read and recite this samādhi sūtra, they need not fear any terrifying events.
Just as those great serpents and various potent poisons can be eliminated by the power of this sutra;
if there be one who receives and upholds this scripture, they shall not fear any evil persons,
yakṣas, rākṣasas, or nāgas, for their followers will never find an opportunity to prevail.
If one constantly guards and makes offerings [to this practice], then in the araṇya one will find companions among lions,
tigers, wolves, and various beasts, as well as rhinoceroses, jackals, leopards, and wild dogs.
If one can protect and uphold this samādhi, That person will possess an invincible power;
They will remain far removed from all those with evil minds, As well as from yakṣas who devour vital essence.
If one can explain this samādhi, they shall be free from all illnesses, obstacles, and calamities;
the eyes received as karmic retribution will never decline, and their speech shall be pure and subtle with great eloquence.
If a person realizes the profound and tranquil dhyāna, their body will be robust and free from all ailments;
throughout this life they shall forever be rid of all unwholesome appearances, and in the end, they will have no fear of the path to hell.
If there are those who can read this scripture of samādhi, the devas will protect them, as will the nāgas and spirits, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and even their enemies;
though evil may approach them, they shall not be startled or afraid.
If one can preach this sutra for others, humans, nāgas, and yakṣas will all rejoice;
the devas will constantly sing its praises day and night, and all World-Honored Ones will cherish them as their own children.
If a person constantly recites this for others and has no doubts regarding any phenomena, their physical appearance will be peerless; how could they ever regress from awakening?
If one can further teach and transform all sentient beings, even when encountering an evil king, civil unrest among the people,
or times of severe drought and soaring grain prices, they shall never suffer affliction or famine.
If a person explains this samādhi, its merits will be inconceivable;
even if Māra were to harass all sentient beings, he could not move a single hair on such a person.
As I have previously said, for those who uphold this sutra, neither various afflictions, terrors,
nor mental defilements shall ever be able to cause them harm, except for the calamities of past karma that were already fixed.
If there are those who protect and uphold this sutra, they shall be my eldest sons;
I have already praised them, and I shall do so again in future ages.
If you can uphold such a Dharma as this, you should constantly give rise to a heart of joy;
together, propagate it and do not abandon it—this is what I now say for your sake.

Chapter Nine: On Benefiting Others. From the *Bhadrapāla-bodhisattva-parivarta* of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, Chapter Nine: On Benefiting Others. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying: “Bhadrapāla!”

I recall that in the past, more than incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Vīrarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, there was a son of a householder named Sudatta, who, together with twenty thousand people, went to the presence of that Buddha, King Fearlessness.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One;
having completed his respectful salutation, he withdrew to sit to one side.
Then Sudatta immediately requested that the Tathāgata Vītarāgarāja extensively proclaim the profound meaning of this samādhi. "Bhadrapāla!

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vītarāgarāja, knowing that the son of the elder possessed deep faith and a desire to hear this samādhi, expounded it for him at the appropriate time in accordance with his needs."
Bhadrapāla!
At that time, after Sudatta had heard this samādhi from that Buddha, he recited it, received and upheld it, contemplated its meaning, and practiced exactly according to the teaching.

Having completed his practice, he returned to that very Dharma of the Tathāgata Abhayarāja, where he left the household life to become a renunciant, shaved off his hair and beard, and donned the saffron robes.
For eighty thousand years, he contemplated and maintained this samādhi, and furthermore, in the presence of that Tathāgata Fearless King, he heard all dharmas and received and upheld them all.

Thereafter, he again encountered various Tathāgatas and heard them preach this Dharma, which he was able to uphold in its entirety. Having planted roots of goodness under those Buddhas and extensively accomplished inconceivable merits, he then, at the end of his life, immediately attained rebirth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where he shared in the same karmic fruition.

“In that very kalpa, he again encountered a second Tathāgata—a Tathāgata born into the Kṣatriya caste who left the household life and attained enlightenment—named Vidyuddatta Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Furthermore, within the Dharma of that Vidyuddatta Tathāgata, he left the household life to practice and, after eighty-four thousand years, once again contemplated this samādhi.”

Furthermore, he encountered a third Tathāgata—whom that third Buddha, having been born into a brahmin family, also renounced the world and attained the Way—named Prabhāpāla (Light-King) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He again renounced the world to practice under that Tathāgata, and for eighty-four thousand years, he constantly attained contemplation of this samādhi.
Bhadrapāla!
From that time forward, after more than a hundred kalpas had passed, the elder’s son Sudatta attained the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Bhadrapāla! You should know this: was that son of a householder, Sudatta, at that time anyone else?
He was none other than the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara of the past."
Bhadrapāla!

Therefore, you should know that because the son of a householder, Sudatta, possessed such love for and delight in the Dharma, and furthermore practiced such seeking of the Dharma, he was able to swiftly accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!

You should now observe how much great and vast benefit this King of Samādhis brings to all bodhisattvas and sentient beings; that is to say, it enables them to attain the ground of wisdom of all Buddhas, and further allows them to receive and uphold the ocean of the extensive learning of all Buddhas."
Bhadrapāla! For this reason, you all should diligently seek this samādhi; you should always delight in hearing it, reciting it, receiving and upholding it, contemplating it, and practicing it.

Having heard and received it, you should further recite, uphold, and explain its meaning for others, causing them to diligently seek it, so that they may all hear and receive it, contemplate it with right mindfulness, and practice according to the teaching.
Why is this so? Bhadrapāla!
