If one can diligently seek, read, recite, receive and uphold, mindfully practice, and widely propagate this samādhi, before long one shall realize the wisdom of all Buddhas, the wisdom of all Tathāgatas, the wisdom of great sovereignty, inconceivable wisdom, incomparable wisdom, unequaled wisdom, and the wisdom of all-knowledge, even unto attaining that wisdom which is not shared with others.
“Bhadrapāla! If there is anyone who can skillfully proclaim this, they should speak correctly thus:
‘This samādhi is the eye of all bodhisattvas, the father of all bodhisattvas, and the mother of all bodhisattvas; it is that which bestows upon all bodhisattvas the wisdom of the Buddhas.’”
"Bhadrapāla! One who speaks thus has well spoken at the proper time; this is the well-spoken exposition of this samādhi. Bhadrapāla!"
Furthermore, if there are any men or women who are able to explain this well at the proper time, they should speak correctly thus:

"This samādhi is the Buddha-nature; it is the Dharma-nature; it is the Saṃgha-nature; it is the stage of the Buddha; it is the ocean of great learning; it is the inexhaustible treasury of dhūta practices; it is the inexhaustible treasury of the merit of dhūta practices; it is the inexhaustible treasury of the merits of all Buddhas; it is the inexhaustible treasury that can give rise to profound patience; it is that which can give rise to great loving-kindness, can give rise to great compassion, and can give rise to bodhi."
"Bhadrapāla! This is how he skillfully explains this samādhi when it is the proper time to do so. Bhadrapāla!"
Furthermore, if there is anyone who can skillfully proclaim this samādhi, they should speak correctly thus:
"This King of Samādhis is able to shatter the darkness of all dharmas and is able to produce the great light of all dharmas."
"Bhadrapāla! This is what is called that 'skillful exposition of samādhi. Bhadrapāla!"

You should observe this Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of Mindfulness of the Buddha, which brings great benefit to all sentient beings; even all the other Bodhisattvas dwelling in this land universally behold all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in all worlds throughout the ten directions, and having gone to the abodes of those Buddhas, they respectfully prostrate, listen to the True Dharma, and make offerings to the Sangha, yet remain free from attachment.
Bhadrapāla!
For this reason, if bodhisattvas wish to accomplish the king of samādhis, they should always observe those four foundations of mindfulness with single-minded diligence.
“Bhadrapāla! How does a bodhisattva contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness?
Bhadrapāla!”
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should always single-mindedly observe the activity of the body, yet ultimately not perceive any body at all;
they should always single-mindedly observe the activity of sensation, yet likewise not perceive any sensation at all;
they should always with one mind observe the activity of the mind, yet likewise not perceive any mind at all.
One should always observe the practice of the Dharma with a single-minded focus, yet not perceive any phenomena at all.
O Bhadrapāla! Who among them could believe such matters as these?
"Only those Arhats who have exhausted their outflows and those Bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive [are exempt]. O Bhadrapāla!

Among them, all foolish and deluded ordinary beings, while practicing this Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of the Buddhas, should constantly contemplate the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, without giving rise to attachment."
Furthermore, he reflects that although the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have preached such a Dharma, they themselves do not cling to it;
he further reflects:
"Having heard this Dharma, I must not cling to anything whatsoever."
Why is this so, Bhadrapāla?
Because all phenomena are empty, being originally unarisen.
Bhadrapāla!
All dharmas are not to be recollected, because there is no locus for recollection.
Bhadrapāla!
All phenomena are detached, for they transcend the thoughts of mind and intellect.
O Bhadrapāla!
All phenomena cannot be grasped, for in suchness there is nothing to be attained.
Bhadrapāla!
All dharmas are unstained, for they are like space.
Bhadrapāla!
All phenomena are pure, for they are far removed from sentient beings.
O Bhadrapāla!
All phenomena are free from turbidity, for their causes and conditions have ceased.
Bhadrapāla!
All phenomena are unconditioned, because a person (pudgala) cannot be apprehended.
Bhadrapāla!
All phenomena are the very nature of nirvāṇa, because their intrinsic nature is pure. Bhadrapāla!
All phenomena are non-existent, because no entity whatsoever can be apprehended.
“Bhadrapāla! Therefore, if bodhisattvas wish to contemplate this samādhi, they cannot enter it through divergent characteristics, for there is no characteristic of attainment;
they must see all Buddhas, maintain right mindfulness of all Buddhas, and remain in harmonious correspondence with them.”
Furthermore, one attains the contemplation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), recollecting and hearing the true Dharma;
one deliberates upon, discriminates, and selects these factors of enlightenment, yet perceives no self and does not realize any phenomena.
Why is this so? Bhadrapāla!
Within this, one cannot perceive the Buddha by means of the characteristic of form, nor can one [perceive him] by means of the characteristic of sound.
One cannot hear the Dharma; one cannot accomplish the *dānapāramitā* with a mind of expectation;
one cannot fulfill the *śīlapāramitā* by delighting in and clinging to the various realms of existence (*bhava*); one cannot attain *nirvāṇa* through stinginess or the concealment of the Dharma;
one cannot acquire great learning (*bahuśruta*) by being deeply attached to the notion of a person (*pudgala*). One cannot...
One cannot rely on conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) while remaining detached from all phenomena; one cannot realize the fruit of enlightenment by dwelling with attachment to pleasure;
one cannot admonish others for their transgressions while following after craving;
one cannot achieve the various forms of patience while constantly delighting in strife; and one cannot obtain wholesome fruits while constantly engaging in unwholesome deeds. Not...
One cannot realize the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle;
nor can one attain the various Bodhisattva patiences (kṣānti); nor can one attain the Samādhi of Emptiness through jealousy or attachment;
nor can one enter śamatha by practicing sensual desire; nor can one realize it through indolence or laziness.
“Noble Guardian! Regarding all the noble paths, one cannot even achieve contemplation without relinquishing various external objects and divergent thoughts.”

Therefore, I now entrust this samādhi to the various celestial kings of the world to receive, uphold, and protect; I also entrust it to you to proclaim in the future, ensuring that it never be severed.

Then, as the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma, eight nayutas of devaputras from the desire and form realms all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people also resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"Nevertheless, all these individuals shall, after the passing of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, fully attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they shall all share the same name, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha Rightly Liberated, dwelling in the world to teach and transform, with lifespans that are likewise equal."

“Bhadrapāla! Since even by merely generating this initial thought of awakening one attains such immeasurable merit and fully accomplishes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how much more so for those who made offerings to me when I was practicing the path of awakening in the past—would they not surely and swiftly accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”

“Bhadrapāla! Furthermore, there were immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, attained the pure eye of wisdom; additionally, eight hundred bhikṣus attained liberation of the mind from all outflows.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Who shall receive and uphold this samādhi?
Their accumulation of merit shall be immeasurable; The conduct of their precepts will be free from dust and defilement, And their fundamental mind pure like a mirror."
Who shall receive and uphold this samādhi?
With vast and boundless erudition reaching to the infinite, their wisdom will be spontaneous and without deficiency, and their merit will be full and bright like the moon.
Who shall receive and uphold this samādhi?
Such a person shall behold the inconceivable Buddhas and, through wisdom, observe the rare Dharma; such inconceivable persons shall all be protected and sustained.
Who shall receive and uphold this samādhi?
Having seen immeasurable World-Honored Ones in the past, whose Dharma teachings were difficult to fathom, they shall all reverently follow them and practice making offerings.
Whoever is able to receive and uphold this samādhi shall become a lamp for the world;
with such great compassion as this, they shall uproot the sufferings of all beings and make offerings to every World-Honored One.
Who is able to receive and uphold this samādhi?
If there are bodhisattvas who wish to see the countless holy Honored Ones of the future, they should cultivate offerings with pure faith.
Who is able to receive and uphold this samādhi?
Such a person will obtain inconceivable and supreme benefits; they will be well-able to take birth among humans and will always succeed in leaving the household life to seek food with virtue.
Who can uphold this samādhi?
Such a person will receive inconceivable and manifold merit, and being able to maintain it into the future, shall obtain the ultimate benefit of these virtues.

Chapter Ten: The Chapter on the Five Dharmas. From the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the Section of Bhadrapāla. At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I only pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will deign to visit my home at the time of the morning meal tomorrow and accept my offerings, out of compassion for us and all sentient beings.
The World-Honored One accepted Bhadrapāla’s request by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, Bhadrapāla prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then took his leave to return. He then proceeded once more to where the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī was staying.
Having arrived, she prostrated at the feet of the bhikṣuṇī Pajāpatī and immediately said:
"I pray that the Noble Lady and the assembly of nuns, out of compassion for me, will accept the modest offering I have prepared for tomorrow morning."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī accepted the invitation in silence.
Knowing this, Bhadrapāla prostrated, took his leave, and returned.
Then Bhadrapāla went again to where Ratnākara, the son of a Licchavi, was and said to him:
“Ratnaśrī! Come here.

I request that you, along with all your kinsmen, relatives, friends, and acquaintances, as well as the assembly of upāsakas in this gathering, and even all those newly arrived from the great city of Rājagṛha and other cities, towns, and villages, accept the meal I have prepared for tomorrow morning.”
At that time, the Licchavi youth Ratnaśrī, having accepted Bhadrapāla’s words, addressed the upāsakas, kinsmen, and retinue present in the assembly, saying:
"Gentlemen, you should know that the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla has instructed me to tell you:
'Please accept my humble offering at the time of the midday meal tomorrow.'"

At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Licchavi Ratnākara, the elder Śreṣṭhin Ghaṭīkāra, the householder’s son Naladatta Māṇava, the elder Varuṇa, along with all their other attendants, friends, and acquaintances, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned to the residence of the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla.

Having arrived, he assisted Bhadrapāla in his management; that very night, he instructed his household to prepare various kinds of exquisite and superior delicacies—namely, every kind of food and drink available in the world, possessing a hundred varieties of color, fragrance, and flavor—and even for poor beggars who had come from distant foreign lands, he prepared various fine meals and provided them, treating them as equals with no distinction from the great assembly.
Why is this? It is because all Bodhisattvas have no hatred or attachment in their hearts and do not dare to disparage others, for they regard all sentient beings with equanimity.

At that time, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, up to Śakra Devānām-indra, the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Four Great Kings such as Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and the divine son Kalyāṇakārin together with his retinue, all assumed human forms to assist in this matter, desiring to cause Bhadrapāla’s fruition of bodhi to be swiftly accomplished.

At that time, Bhadrapāla, together with his retinue, virtuous friends, and spiritual mentors, swept and sprinkled their own home as well as the streets and roads of the great city of Rājagṛha. In every place, they hung exquisite banners and canopies and extensively arranged various kinds of ornaments to adorn them. Furthermore, they scattered various subtle flowers and incenses upon the ground and burned the foremost incense in the world as an offering.

Then, having thus adorned the great city of Rājagṛha and prepared the exquisite food, Bhadrapāla went to the place where the World-Honored One was with his retinue at dawn; prostrating with his head at the Buddha's feet, he addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"My task is accomplished; please know that this is the time.

Then, at the hour of dawn—for the sake of Bhadrapāla—the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and, surrounded on all sides by an immeasurable assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, gods, humans, and others, proceeded toward the residence of the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla.
Thereupon, Bhadrapāla had this thought:
"My home is narrow and small, unable to accommodate such a great multitude.

Would it not be most wonderful if, through the majestic power and protection of the World-Honored One, my house were made vast and entirely of lapis lazuli, so that all the people within the city could see it clearly, and so that this present assembly of devas and humans might enjoy it as they please without any lack?"

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in Bhadrapāla’s mind, immediately employed his supernatural power to cause the house to become magnificent, spacious, and vast, and to transform all its furnishings into lapis lazuli. He further caused all the people within the city to see it clearly and distinctly, providing the great assembly with sufficient means to use it as they pleased.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the house of Bhadrapāla and sat down calmly upon his seat; he likewise had all the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and the great assembly of humans and devas sit down in their respective orders according to their classes.

At that time, when the World-Honored One and the fourfold assembly of gods and humans had all taken their seats, Bhadrapāla, the Licchavi Ratnākara, the upāsaka Śreṣṭhin Ghaṭikāra, and the merchant’s son Naradatta, seeing this, personally took the most exquisite food with their own hands and offered it to the World-Honored One.

Having accepted it, the World-Honored One then bestowed various superior, fragrant, and delicious foods upon the fourfold assembly and the entire multitude of gods and humans, allowing them all to partake to their heart's content until everyone was fully satisfied.

Thus, when all the food had been consumed, and they had finished washing their hands, rinsing their mouths, and even cleaning and putting away the alms bowls, Bhadrapāla set aside a small seat, prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One before him, and then withdrew to sit with single-minded devotion gazing up at him.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Licchavi Ratnākara, the lay follower Śreṣṭhin Ghaṭīkāra, the young brahmin Naradatta, and the great assembly of the fourfold community of gods and humans, preached the Dharma as was appropriate so that they might understand it; he guided, exhorted, and comforted them, causing them to rejoice. Thereafter, together with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and the great assembly of gods and humans, he returned to his original dwelling place.

Then, after the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla had finished his meal, he was surrounded on all sides by his retinue, virtuous friends, spiritual mentors, and a multitude of hundreds of thousands; he approached the World-Honored One, paid respectful homage, withdrew to sit to one side, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Bhadrapāla, how many dharmas must a bodhisattva-mahāsattva fulfill in order to be able to realize this samādhi of presence?
The Buddha said:
"Bhadrapāla!"
If a bodhisattva can accomplish five dharmas, they will then attain this samādhi of presence before one's eyes.
What are these five?
They are as follows:
First, possessing profound patience, they eliminate [afflictions] until they reach exhaustion;
second, in reality there is nothing to be exhausted, nor is there any place of exhaustion;
third, originally there is no disorder, yet they eliminate all disorder.
Fourth, they are originally without defilement and eliminate all defilements;
fifth, they are originally without dust and sever all attachment to dust.
O Bhadrapāla!

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully accomplished the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), is able to attain this samādhi of presence before one's eyes.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
Furthermore, there are five dharmas by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can attain samādhi:
first, profound revulsion toward all states of existence and non-acceptance of all conditioned formations;
second, maintaining mindfulness of the bodhicitta in all places of birth.
Third, wherever they are born, they shall always see the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
fourth, they shall never be attached to the aggregates, elements, or sense bases;
fifth, they shall never crave or cling to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
"Bhadrapāla!
These are the five dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva must fulfill to achieve this samādhi.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"
Furthermore, there are five dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva can attain samādhi:
first, one should constantly contemplate the mind that is without limit;
second, one should always be able to skillfully enter meditative concentration and engage in contemplation.
Third, to analytically contemplate all phenomena;
fourth, to be free from a contentious mind toward sentient beings;
and fifth, to constantly gather and sustain sentient beings through the four means of attraction—namely, giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation.
"Bhadrapāla!
These are the five dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the samādhi.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"
Furthermore, there are five dharmas by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can attain samādhi:
first, constantly practicing a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings;
second, at all times, mindfully cultivating noble conduct.
Third, they constantly practice patience and always give rise to a heart of reverence when seeing those who violate the precepts;
fourth, they do not speak of their own abilities in the presence of their own upādhyāyas and ācāryas;
fifth, they never dare to disparage others in any situation.
"Bhadrapāla!
These are the five dharmas which, when fully possessed by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, enable them to realize this samādhi of presence before one.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"
Furthermore, there are five dharmas by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can attain samādhi:
first, constantly relying on the holy teachings and practicing according to what is taught;
second, purifying the mental karma and extinguishing the evils of body and speech.
Third, maintaining pure ethical conduct and severing all views;
fourth, constantly seeking extensive learning and having deep faith in all that is wholesome;
fifth, constantly recollecting the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Bhadrapāla!
These are the five dharmas which, when fully possessed by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, enable them to attain the samādhi of presence.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"
Furthermore, there are five dharmas by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can attain samādhi:

first, constantly practicing great giving, acting as a donor, not giving rise to stinginess or greed, having no jealousy in the heart, extensively and broadly bestowing gifts with a mind that is pure, straightforward, and free from flattery.

Toward all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, the poor, the solitary, and all beggars, he had nothing he would not cherish; there was no superior or precious object that he did not give away—namely, all kinds of exquisite food and drink, famous garments and fine robes, the finest dwellings, various types of bedding, lamps and candles, flowers and incense; indeed, he relinquished everything he possessed for use.
Although they constantly practice giving, they do not seek reward; they have compassion for all beings with a mind free from doubt, and once they have given, they never feel regret.

Second, they always act as donors by practicing the gift of Dharma—meaning they constantly preach such a teaching to sentient beings, which is said to be foremost, supreme, most excellent, most wondrous, and most refined.
When practicing such a great gift of Dharma, one is able to produce all forms of unimpeded eloquence, with the sequence of words and meanings continuing without interruption.
One is able to dwell securely within and achieve profound patience regarding the extremely deep teachings spoken by the Tathāgata.

At times, even when subjected by others to slander, verbal abuse, beating, or flogging, they never harbor resentment, defilement, or a poisonous mind; nor do they experience fear or various forms of suffering, but remain fearless in heart and always maintain a sense of joy.

Third, when hearing others speak of this samādhi, one listens with a sincere mind, receives it, copies it, recites it, contemplates its meaning, and extensively explains and expounds it for others, so that this sublime Dharma may long abide in the world, never concealing it to cause the Dharma to perish prematurely.

Fourth, they are always free from envy and far removed from all afflictions; having cast off the hindrances and entanglements and severed the dust and defilements, they neither praise themselves nor disparage others.

Fifth, one should always maintain profound faith toward all Buddhas, always practice reverence and awe toward all teachers and elders, always give rise to a sense of shame and remorse in the presence of spiritual friends, and always harbor compassion for the young; even when receiving a small kindness from another, one still thinks of repaying it generously—how much more so when someone possesses great virtue, how could one dare to forget it?
He always speaks words of truth and has never uttered falsehoods.
O Bhadrapāla!
It is by being endowed with these five dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to attain such a samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"If one’s mind desires and delights in the profound Dharma, And feels weary of and detached from all future existences, The wise do not wish for any form of birth;
If one can act thus, they shall attain samādhi."
One need not rely on any external treatises, nor should one listen to or accept even their words; by forever severing the five worldly desires, if one can thus realize samādhi.
Pure in the observance of precepts and abiding in the holy life, Not thinking of women wherever one is born,
Deeply wearying of the five desires, such a true son of the Buddha— If one can act thus, one shall realize this samādhi.
Constantly practicing great giving without seeking reward, And without any mind of attachment or regret;
Once having relinquished, not dwelling on it again, One should only collect the mind to contemplate the Buddhas.
When practicing giving out of compassion for sentient beings, One resolutely eliminates doubt without wavering or retreating.
Abiding in gentleness and practicing giving, if one can do so, one will attain this samādhi.
If one is a great master in the giving of wealth, free from pride and envy,
and always joyful in performing every act of charity— if one can do so, one will attain this samādhi.
Furthermore, being foremost in the gift of Dharma, Skillfully understanding the subtle sūtras,
Able to know the profound dharma of quiescence— If one can act thus, one shall attain samādhi.
Abiding securely within all profound dharmas, Skillfully enduring with no jealousy,
Even when beaten or reviled, remaining free from resentment— If one can thus practice, they shall attain this samādhi.
If at some time one hears this sutra being preached, and copies it, reads and recites it, or skillfully proclaims it widely—
doing so solely for the sake of the endurance of the Dharma and the benefit of the world— one will be able to attain this samādhi.
Not being stingy or secretive regarding any dharmas, seeking neither profit nor fame,
but solely for the sake of perpetuating the lineage of all Buddhas— if one can thus practice, one shall realize this samādhi.
Far removed from sleep and the afflictions of decay, having severed jealousy and the fetters of the hindrances,
not praising oneself nor disparaging others— one can extinguish the mark of self and attain samādhi.
With right faith in the Buddhas, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, Always acting with sincerity and free from deceit,
Never forgetting to repay all kindness received— Such a person will realize samādhi without difficulty;
If one can speak truly and without falsehood, Whatever they do will likewise never fail.
Though the deed performed may be small, the reward obtained is vast; they encounter no obstacles in realizing the Dharma.

If a person is able to possess these qualities—maintaining pure precepts and protecting those who have shown kindness—then even attaining Bodhi is not difficult for them, let alone the profound and subtle meditative concentration.

11. Chapter on the Prediction: The Section on Bhadrapāla from the Mahāsannipāta Sūtra, Chapter Eleven: The Prediction. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying: "Bhadrapāla!"
I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and further beyond immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I first heard this samādhi from the presence of the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara;
having heard it, I immediately realized such a samādhi and beheld all Tathāgatas ever present before me.
From that time until now, I have passed through the presence of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya World-Honored Ones, receiving this sutra from them all and practicing it with offerings.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestowed upon me this prediction: "Māṇava!

In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

“Bhadrapāla! You all should likewise apply yourselves with diligence, contemplate with single-minded focus, and cultivate such noble dharmas—which are not the realm perceived by ordinary persons, but are profoundly deep, tranquil, and the place where all signs cease.
Having trained in this way, you will naturally achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the future without difficulty, no different from me.”
"You should all know that if there are those who abide in this samādhi, they will naturally attain proximity to great bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"In the past, I encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; Having seen him, I immediately attained samādhi."
From now on you shall constantly behold all Tathāgatas, Those of great renown, fully endowed with merit.
If you merely accumulate many merits And focus your mind with single-minded recollection, you will attain success;
If a person can practice within this Dharma, They shall surely attain the path of unsurpassed Bodhi.
Chapter Twelve: Profundity. From the *Bhadrapāla-parivarta* of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, Chapter Twelve: Profundity. At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How should one contemplate this samādhi?
The Buddha said,
"Bhadrapāla!"

If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to contemplate and cultivate this samādhi, when observing those forms they should not grasp at them; they should not grasp at those sounds, they should not grasp at those odors, they should not grasp at those tastes, they should not grasp at those tangibles, they should not grasp at any phenomena (*dharma*), they should not grasp at any births, and they should not grasp at any locations. Within these dharmas, they should give rise to the practice of true and great compassion.
Among these, what is called samādhi?
It is the practice in accordance with the Dharma regarding all phenomena.
When Bodhisattvas contemplate the foundations of mindfulness, they should act in this way:

Observing the activities of the body, one ultimately does not conceptually differentiate or perceive a locus for bodily activity; observing the activities of sensation, one likewise does not conceptually differentiate or perceive a locus for the activity of sensation; observing the activities of the mind, one likewise does not conceptually differentiate or perceive a locus for mental activity; and observing the activities of phenomena, one likewise does not conceptually differentiate or perceive a locus for the activity of phenomena. A bodhisattva should thus observe and contemplate samādhi.
Why is this? Bhadrapāla!
When that bodhisattva contemplates bodily formations, he does not give rise to conceptualization or discrimination regarding the body.
When observing the activity of sensation, one does not give rise to discursive thought or discrimination regarding sensation;
when observing the activity of the mind, one does not give rise to discursive thought or discrimination regarding the mind;
and when observing the activity of phenomena, one does not give rise to discursive thought or discrimination regarding phenomena.
Why is this? Because all phenomena (*dharma*) are unattainable.
Thus, since all phenomena are unattainable, how could there be any conceptualization or discursive thought?
Bhadrapāla!
Therefore, all phenomena are without discrimination;
that which is without discrimination is without conceptualization.
One who is without conceptualization should know that within it there is no dharma to be seen.
O Bhadrapāla!
Because there is nothing to be seen, it is unimpeded; because there is no obstruction among all dharmas, this is precisely the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Presence.

Because the Bodhisattva accomplishes this samādhi, he immediately beholds immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and hears all that they proclaim. Having heard those teachings, he is able to receive and uphold all the unimpeded liberations and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; he also immediately attains that unimpeded wisdom.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
When a bodhisattva contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness, no phenomenon is to be seen and no sound is to be heard.

Because there is nothing seen or heard, there is no phenomenon that can be differentiated, nor is there any phenomenon that can be contemplated; yet, this is not because one is like those who are blind or deaf, but simply because all phenomena have nothing that can be seen."
Therefore, when observing [time], one does not give rise to attachment while perceiving the various paths;
by contemplating the path, one becomes free from the net of doubt regarding all phenomena;
being free from the net of doubt, one beholds the Buddha, the Tathāgata.
Because one beholds the Tathāgata, one is forever freed from delusion and error;
because there is no delusion or error, one knows that all phenomena ultimately cannot be seen. Why is this?
If a bodhisattva possesses such views, they grasp at those views;
because they grasp at those views, they grasp at the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa);
because they grasp at the characteristics of phenomena, they grasp at activities.
Because of grasping at activities, one perceives sentient beings;
because of perceiving sentient beings, one perceives a life span;
because of perceiving a life span, one perceives a person (pudgala).
Because one sees the person (pudgala), one sees the aggregates (skandhas);
because one sees the aggregates, one sees the sense bases (āyatanas);
because one sees the sense bases, one sees the elements (dhātus).
By seeing the various realms, one sees their characteristics;
by seeing their characteristics, one sees the various objects;
by seeing the various objects, one sees their causes.
Because one sees that cause, one further sees the conditions;
because one sees the conditions, one then seeks and grasps;
because of seeking and grasping, there is birth and existence.
Why is this? Bhadrapāla!
All dharmas can ultimately never be grasped.
Because there is nothing to be grasped, the bodhisattva does not conceptualize, does not dwell upon, does not see, and does not hear any of those dharmas.
"Bhadrapāla! This is ultimately superior to the grasping and attachment to the *pudgala* and the view of self held by the non-Buddhists or their disciples."
Bhadrapāla!
A bodhisattva never forms such a view.
What is that view?
When a bodhisattva sees, it is as the Tathāgata sees, and they never regress;
a bodhisattva’s seeing is like the seeing of a pratyekabuddha and like the seeing of an arhat—a bodhisattva should indeed cultivate such a way of seeing.
Seeing things in this way, one does not recollect, does not think, does not see, and does not hear;
because of this lack of recollection, thought, seeing, and hearing, all deluded imaginings are extinguished, and one immediately attains the contemplation of this samādhi.

"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla! It is like space, which from the beginning has no form or color and cannot be seen; it is without obstruction, without dependence, and without a place of abiding; it is pure and unstained, and free from turbidity.

When Bodhisattvas perceive all dharmas, it is also like this: within all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, there is no obstruction or even no location whatsoever. Because their eyes are pure and unobstructed, all dharmas naturally manifest before them."

When those bodhisattvas were thus reflecting, they immediately beheld the Buddhas. Their magnificent adornments were like golden litters, complete with majestic deportment; they were like hundreds of thousands of flames blazing with brilliant light; they were like the full autumn moon surrounded by a multitude of stars; they were like the military host of a wheel-turning monarch, fierce and powerful; they were like Śakra, Lord of Devas, the most honored among his four ministers; they were like the Great Brahmā King seated upon his celestial throne; they were like a lion king whose majesty subdues all other beasts; they were like a pure white swan flying through the sky; they were like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, firmly established in the great ocean; they were like the Great Snowy Mountains producing various excellent medicines; they were like the Iron Ring Mountains containing the violent winds; they were like the element of water supporting the great earth; they were like the great wind-circle purifying the realm of space; and they were like the magnificent celestial palaces atop Mount Sumeru.
In this way, Bhadrapāla!
Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas illuminate all the Buddha-worlds of the trichiliocosm with the light of their wisdom and virtue; such is the manner of their activity.
"Bhadrapāla! Within their correct contemplation, those bodhisattvas further reflect in this way:
'Whatever the Tathāgatas have proclaimed, I have heard it in the past;'"
Having heard it, they shall read, recite, receive, uphold, and practice it.
Having reflected thus, he arose from samādhi and contemplated the meaning of all those dharmas as he had heard them within that concentration, and proclaimed them for others.

"Bhadrapāla, you should know that this King of Samādhis brings about such benefits for all bodhisattvas, and is able to bestow such a mass of merits, namely, all dharmas, both mundane and supramundane."
Bhadrapāla! Therefore, if those sons or daughters of good family wish to realize unexcelled bodhi according to their aspiration, they should listen to this samādhi;

having heard it, they should copy it, read and recite it, receive and uphold it, cultivate and contemplate it, and explain it extensively to others, so that this sublime Dharma may circulate throughout the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“The Buddhas are pure and free from dust and defilement; Their merit is profound and vast, having no dependence.
With the resonant clanging of bells and drums and myriad wondrous sounds, All ten thousand kinds of things are prepared to cultivate offerings.”
Scattering various kinds of world-transcending incense, Exquisite and extraordinary flower garlands and supreme jeweled canopies,
And lighting lamps as offerings to the many shrines and temples— All these were done for the sake of seeking this samādhi.
The Buddha-dharma is profoundly deep and difficult to perceive; it reveals the conventional truth so that people may know it.
That [truth] is like intrinsic nature, originally unchanging; you should follow this accordingly with unimpeded wisdom.
Just as when the sun and moon first emerge, and Śakra, the Lord of Devas, together with the thirty-two gods,
are adorned with all manner of magnificent ornaments in perfect abundance— seeking that samādhi is likewise so.
Just as Brahmā dwells among the Brahma-hosts, his deportment serene and his merit perfected,
his courageous diligence beyond measure— so too is the one who seeks samādhi.
Furthermore, like a king of physicians dwelling in the world, who bestows a multitude of wondrous medicines upon the sick,
he accords with the pure minds of all Buddhas, never for a moment departing from the fundamental nature of emptiness.
Like the Snowy Mountains, the king of all mountains, resplendent like a universal monarch (cakravartin),
and like a precious palanquin exquisitely adorned— thus do they behold the Buddhas, complete with all their marks. Furthermore,
like the king of swans, pure white, moving freely and without obstruction through the sky.
Thus do the sons of the World-Honored One contemplate the golden bodies of all Buddhas.
With the lamp of pure wisdom from the stainless samādhi, they are able to shatter the great gloom of all darkness.
Having eliminated all perceptions of objective things, they contemplate the unimpeded light of the Buddhas' wisdom.
All defilements are extinguished and the poison of hatred is gone;
for the person of pure and wondrous wisdom who is both enlightened and clear, if they can contemplate that there is neither self nor other, they shall ultimately have no perception of material forms.
Within the state free from doubt, pure wisdom arises; it is able to sever all views of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, the perceptions of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*) have already been extinguished; hearing the Dharma removes affliction and brings about refreshing clarity.
Monks, you should know that all sons of the Buddha, as well as pure bhikṣuṇīs,
and those upāsakas and upāsikās, can attain this samādhi if they are able to keep it in mind.
The Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, Scroll Four;
The Bhadrapāla Section of the Mahāsaṃnipāta Mahāyāna Sūtra, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen: The Ten Dharmas within the Samādhi of Presence.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying: "Bhadrapāla!"
If there is a bhikṣu who desires to cultivate this samādhi, he should first contemplate that perception of signlessness;
once he has contemplated it, the conceit of "I" will not arise.
“Bhadrapāla! Having eliminated arrogance and pride, with a mind at ease and far removed from all signs,
you should then proclaim this samādhi to others and must not give rise to contention.”
In this context, what is meant by "dispute"?
It refers to conceptual construction and slander; specifically, to revile emptiness is called dispute.
O Bhadrapāla!
Therefore, because he is free from contention, that bhikṣu should be able to cultivate and train in this samādhi and proclaim it to others. "Bhadrapāla!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to cultivate and train in this samādhi and explain it to others, they should fully accomplish ten dharmas before explaining this samādhi to others."
What are these ten?
They are as follows:
first, those sons and daughters of good family first subdue their pride and give rise to a mind of reverence;
Second, to know gratitude and not forget it, constantly keeping in mind the desire to repay it;
third, for the mind to be free from attachment and devoid of envy;
fourth, to eliminate and sever doubt as well as all obstacles.
Fifth, having deep and indestructible faith, one maintains focused mindfulness and contemplation;
sixth, with diligent and energetic pursuit, one practices walking meditation without weariness;
seventh, one always subsists on almsfood and does not accept special invitations.
Eighth, having few desires and being content, with the sense faculties subdued;
ninth, possessing right faith in the profound *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the forbearance that all phenomena are non-arising);
tenth, constantly mindful:
"Who possesses this samādhi?
Thinking thus, one should conceive of that teacher as a Buddha, and only then practice such a samādhi.
O Bhadrapāla!

When those good sons and good daughters have fulfilled these ten kinds of dharmas as described above, they should practice this samādhi and cause others to receive, uphold, read, and recite it as well.
“A practitioner who acts in this way shall attain eight things. What are these eight?
First, ultimate purity, because they do not violate any of the prohibitive precepts.”
Second, the purity of knowledge and vision, because wisdom is integrated and does not correspond with anything else;
third, the purity of wisdom, because one no longer undergoes further existence in subsequent births;
fourth, the purity of giving, because one does not desire the karmic fruits and retributions of any conditioned phenomena.
Fifth is the purity of extensive learning, because having heard the Dharma, one never forgets it;
sixth is the purity of diligence, because at all times one seeks the Bodhi of the Buddha;
seventh is the purity of detachment, because one is unstained by and does not cling to any fame or profit.
Eighth is the purity of non-retrogression, because one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without being shaken at the outset.
O Bhadrapāla!
These are the eight dharmas obtained by those sons and daughters of good family.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"The wise person does not give rise to perceptions of marks; They should also eliminate pride and the notion of self.
Within profound patience, they have no grasping or attachment; Such a person can swiftly proclaim this samādhi."
In the void, the roots of contention have been extinguished from the beginning; Nirvāṇa is signless, the great tranquil samādhi.
Those who harbor no resentment toward the Buddha and do not slander the Dharma Can swiftly proclaim this samādhi.
The wise do not give rise to thoughts of envy or jealousy; Mindful of the Buddha, they recognize the debt of gratitude toward the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
That which is born subdues [the afflictions] without wavering; Thus they maintain this tranquil samādhi.
Free from jealousy and without doubt, They contemplate the profound Dharma with true faith.
Diligent and tireless, free from all desires, he is thus able to attain samādhi.
Constantly practicing the bhikṣu’s way of begging for food, he renounces all special invitations, let alone seeking wealth;
having severed defilements and realized suchness, he is thus able to attain samādhi.
Who can possess this samādhi?
I should listen to it and cause it to spread widely; by conceiving the thought of a Buddha toward the teacher, one will be able to attain such samādhi.
If a person practices this samādhi, they shall possess merits that transcend the world;
they should swiftly receive the eight kinds of dharmas, which accord with the minds of all Buddhas and are pure and stainless.
With pure ethical discipline that is boundless, With samādhi, awakening, and supreme vision,
They are able to purify all realms of existence, Abiding in a most excellent mass of merit.
With pure wisdom, they do not undergo further existence; through giving, they leave defilement behind and enter the unconditioned.
Having attained that vast learning, they never forget it; such a person is a treasury of the merits of the wise.
Through courageous diligence one attains awakening; One does not crave or become stained by worldly fame and profit.
If the wise practice this well, They enter the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous dhyāna.

Chapter 14: On Unique Qualities. From the *Bhadrapāla-parivarta* of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, Chapter Fourteen: On Unique Qualities. At that time, the Blessed One again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla, saying: "Bhadrapāla!"
Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas shall further accomplish the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
What are called the unique qualities? They are as follows:

from the time the Tathāgata first attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) until his parinirvāṇa, throughout that interval, all the three types of action (*tri-karma*) of the Tathāgata have wisdom as their primary guide; all bodily actions proceed in accordance with wisdom, all verbal actions proceed in accordance with wisdom, and all mental actions proceed in accordance with wisdom.
Furthermore, all Tathāgatas possess unobstructed knowledge and vision of the past, unobstructed knowledge and vision of the future, and unobstructed knowledge and vision of the present.

Moreover, all Tathāgatas act without error, their speech is without lapse, their minds are without forgetfulness, they have no divergent thoughts, they are constantly in samādhi, and there is nothing they do not know before relinquishing it.

Furthermore, all Tathāgatas have no decrease in intention, no decrease in vigor, no decrease in meditative concentration, no decrease in wisdom, no decrease in liberation, and no decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"Bhadrapāla!
These are the eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata; those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice them and bring them to full perfection.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having achieved and perfected this profound and difficult-to-perceive samādhi that embraces the true Dharma, wishes to proclaim it, they should further receive ten kinds of superior dharmas.
What are these ten? They are the so-called ten powers of the Tathāgata.
What are the ten powers?
Bhadrapāla!

Among these, the Tathāgata’s power regarding what is possible and what is impossible is because the Tathāgata, with respect to all matters of what is possible and what is impossible, is able to know them as they truly are through correct wisdom.
Bhadrapāla!

Thus, regarding the matters of what is possible and what is impossible, the Tathāgata is able to know them as they truly are through right knowledge; this is the Tathāgata’s power of the possible and the impossible.

Having attained this power, the Tathāgata knows the place of reality and utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, turning the Great Brahma-wheel—which has never been turned before—and such a wheel as this can never be turned by any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Brahmā, Māra, or human being in the entire world.
"Bhadrapāla!
This is the first power of wisdom of the Tathāgata, which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study, cultivate, and bring to full perfection.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

Among these, the Tathāgata’s power of the knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations means that the Tathāgata, regarding the distinctions among the paths to all destinations, knows them exactly as they are through right wisdom.
Bhadrapāla!

Thus, when the Tathāgata is able to know, through right wisdom, all matters concerning the paths leading to every destination as they truly are, this is the Tathāgata’s power of knowing the paths leading to every destination.

Having attained this power, the Tathāgata knows the place of reality and utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, turning the Great Brahma Wheel—which has never been turned before—and which no one in the world—whether among śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, gods, Brahmās, Māras, or humans—is ever able to turn in such a manner.
“Bhadrapāla!
This is the second power of wisdom of the Tathāgata, which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study, cultivate, and bring to full perfection.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!”

Regarding the Tathāgata’s power over the various elements of the world: it is because the Tathāgata, through correct knowledge, knows as they truly are the infinite distinctions among the various elements in the world.
Bhadrapāla!
Thus, when the Tathāgata knows all the various worldly realms as they truly are through right wisdom, this is the Tathāgata’s power regarding the world-realm.

Having attained this power, the Tathāgata knows the place of ultimate reality; amidst the great assembly, he lets out the lion’s roar and turns the Great Brahma-wheel—which has never been turned before—such that no one in the world, whether among śramaṇas or brahmins, gods, Brahmas, Māras, or humans, will ever be able to turn it in such a manner.
"Bhadrapāla!
This is the third power of knowledge of the Tathāgata, which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study, cultivate, and bring to full perfection.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

Regarding the power of the Tathāgata’s mental activity herein: it is because the Tathāgata, through right knowledge, knows as they truly are the various mental activities of all sentient beings and their immeasurable distinctions.
Bhadrapāla!

In this way, when the Tathāgata is able to know, through right knowledge, the various mental activities of sentient beings in their immeasurable distinctions as they truly are, this is the Tathāgata’s power of knowing mental activities.

Having attained this power, the Tathāgata knows the place of reality and utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, turning the Great Brahma-wheel—which has never been turned before—and which no one in the world—whether among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, Brahmas, Māras, or humans—is ever able to turn in such a manner.
"Bhadrapāla!
This is the fourth power of knowledge of the Tathāgata, which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study, cultivate, and bring to full perfection.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

Regarding the Tathāgata’s power of knowing the differences among the faculties of sentient beings: it is because the Tathāgata knows, with correct wisdom and in accordance with reality, all the various distinctions among the faculties of sentient beings.
Bhadrapāla!

In this way, when the Tathāgata knows, through correct wisdom, the various differences among the faculties of sentient beings as they truly are, this is the Tathāgata’s power of the differentiation of faculties.

Having attained this power, the Tathāgata knows the place of reality and utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, turning the Great Brahma-wheel—which has never been turned before—and such a wheel as this can never be turned by any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas in the world, nor by gods, Brahmās, Māras, or humans.
"Bhadrapāla!
This is the fifth power of knowledge of the Tathāgata, which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study, cultivate, and bring to full perfection.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

Regarding the Tathāgata’s power of meditative concentration therein: the Tathāgata, with respect to all meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis, as well as the arising of afflictions and their cessation, knows them as they truly are through right wisdom.
Bhadrapāla!

In this way, when the Tathāgata knows with correct wisdom, exactly as it is, all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and attainments (*samāpatti*), from the arising of afflictions up to their purification, this is the power of the Tathāgata’s meditative concentration.

Having attained this and known the place of true reality, the Tathāgata lets out a lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and turns the Great Brahma Wheel—a wheel never before turned by anyone in the world, whether among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, Brahmās, Māras, or humans; none shall ever be able to turn it thus.
"Bhadrapāla!
This is the sixth power of knowledge of the Tathāgata, which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study, cultivate, and fully perfect.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

Regarding the Tathāgata’s power of karma: the Tathāgata knows, through his correct wisdom as it truly is, all those various distinctions among karmas, as well as the immeasurable distinctions in their future convergence and the resulting retributions.
Bhadrapāla!

Thus, the various distinctions among these karmas and the corresponding distinctions in the fruits obtained in the future—all these the Tathāgata knows as they truly are through his correct wisdom; this is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the power of karma.

Having attained realization and known the true state of things, the Tathāgata utters a lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and turns the Great Brahma Wheel—a wheel never before turned by anyone in this world, whether among śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Brahmās, Māras, or humans—and no one shall ever be able to turn it as he does.
"Bhadrapāla!
This is the seventh power of action of the Tathāgata, which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study, cultivate, and bring to full perfection.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

Regarding the Tathāgata’s power of the divine eye: the Tathāgata constantly uses his purified divine eye, which surpasses that of human eyes, to see those future multitudes of sentient beings as they die here and are born there; he sees the bodies they receive, whether beautiful or ugly, virtuous or evil; the forms they obtain, whether excellent or inferior, sublime or coarse; whether they are born in the good realms or the evil destinies; and he further sees the various karmas performed by sentient beings, whether virtuous or evil.

There are sentient beings who possess evil karma of body, evil karma of speech, and evil karma of mind; they revile the noble ones, slander the true Dharma, and destroy the harmony of the Saṃgha. Because they are fully possessed of such evil karmas, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they are reborn in the woeful realms.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who possess good karma of body, good karma of speech, and good karma of mind; they revere the noble ones, honor the true Dharma, and make offerings to the Saṃgha. Because they have fully practiced such good karmas, at the end of their lives, they attain rebirth in the auspicious destinies of humans or devas. He knows all such matters exactly as they are.
Bhadrapāla!

With the pure divine eye, the Tathāgata sees all sentient beings as they die here and are reborn there, even unto their passing away and being born in the heavens; this is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth.

Having attained this power and knowing the place of reality, he utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and turns the Great Brahma-wheel—which has never been turned before—such that no one in the world, whether among śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Brahmās, Māras, or humans, shall ever be able to turn it in such a manner.
"Bhadrapāla!
This is the eighth power of knowledge of the Tathāgata, which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice, study, and fully perfect.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

Regarding the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge of past lives: by means of his various knowledges of past lives, the Tathāgata knows all matters of past existences. That is to say, he knows how sentient beings were born here and died there; or how they first received one birth in a certain place, or two, or three, or five, or ten, or a hundred, or a thousand, and even up to receiving immeasurable hundreds of births, immeasurable thousands of births, or immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births. In this manner, he knows as it truly is everything from immeasurable cycles of kalpas, immeasurable fixed kalpas, to immeasurable cycles of kalpas that have turned and those that have not.

Furthermore, regarding the destinies where they are born, such as their place, family, lineage, name, physical appearance, manner of birth, food and drink, activities, virtues and evils, sorrows and joys, and sufferings and pleasures—even down to the duration of their various lifespans—he knows them all as they truly are.

Furthermore, because he fully knows all past events—such as having abandoned that body in a certain place and being reborn in another, with such physical characteristics, such speech, and such experiences, including even the duration of his lifespan.
Bhadrapāla!

When the Tathāgata, by means of various and immeasurable knowledges of past lives, knows the destinies through which those sentient beings have passed—beginning from a single birth up to immeasurable births, and even including all past events throughout their lifespans, knowing them as they truly are—this is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding past lives.

Having attained this power, he stands amidst the great assembly and utters the lion’s roar, turning the Great Brahma-wheel—which has never been turned before—and such as no one in the world—whether among the śramaṇas or brahmins, gods, Brahmās, Māras, or humans—is ever able to turn.
"Bhadrapāla!
This is the ninth power of knowledge of the Tathāgata, which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study, cultivate, and bring to full completion.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"
Regarding the Tathāgata’s power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*): the Tathāgata is able to exhaust all forms of existence, such that there are no further outflows.
Having personally realized the Dharma through liberation of mind and wisdom, he therefore proclaims:
"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall not undergo further existence."
"O Bhadrapāla!
Because the Tathāgata has thus been able to exhaust all outflows (āsrava), and because he has personally realized and known through the clarity of his mind and wisdom, he says:
'My births have been exhausted; I shall not undergo further existence.'"
To know this as it truly is, this is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñānabala*).

Having attained this, the Tathāgata stands amidst the great assembly and lets out a lion’s roar, turning the Great Brahma-wheel—which has never been turned before—such that no one in this world, whether among śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, gods, Brahmās, Māras, or humans, will ever be able to turn it in such a manner.
"Bhadrapāla!
This is the tenth power of knowledge of the Tathāgata, which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study, cultivate, and bring to full completion. Bhadrapāla!"
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas read, recite, receive and uphold, contemplate, and cultivate this samādhi, they will be able to encompass and receive the ten powers of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“The eighteen unique qualities of perfect enlightenment, The ten powers and clear wisdom—these are shared by all Buddhas.
When Bodhisattvas cultivate this wondrous dhyāna, They spontaneously accomplish these two kinds.”

Chapter Fifteen: Merit of Rejoicing. From the *Bhadrapāla-bodhisattva-parivarta* of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, Chapter Fifteen: Merit of Rejoicing. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying: “Bhadrapāla!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva fully accomplishes the four kinds of sympathetic joy, they shall immediately attain this samādhi of presence before one's eyes and swiftly fulfill unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"What are the four kinds of sympathetic joy?
They are as follows: that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should form this thought:

'Just as all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, each when practicing the bodhisattva path in former times, all attained this samādhi by means of sympathetic joy; because of this samādhi, they became fully endowed with great learning, and through great learning, they swiftly accomplished Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"

Just as I am today, so too should it be for others: by relying upon and rejoicing in [the merit], one attains this samādhi; by means of this samādhi, one becomes fully endowed with extensive learning (bahuśruta); and through extensive learning, one swiftly achieves unsurpassed bodhi.
"Bhadrapāla! This is the first mass of merit resulting from sympathetic joy for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Bhadrapāla!"
That bodhisattva-mahāsattva should further reflect in this way:

"Just as all those future Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, when practicing the bodhisattva path, all attained this samādhi through sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), and by means of this samādhi became fully endowed with great learning (*bahuśruta*), and through that great learning swiftly accomplished unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*);

so too shall I today likewise attain this samādhi through sympathetic joy, rely upon this samādhi to seek the fulfillment of great learning, and through that great learning swiftly accomplish that unsurpassed enlightenment."
"Bhadrapāla! This is the second accumulation of merit through sympathetic joy for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Bhadrapāla!"
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva should further reflect in this way:

"At present, in all the infinite, boundless, and incalculable worlds, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas— each of whom, in the past when practicing as a bodhisattva, also attained this samādhi through sympathetic joy (anumodanā), and by means of this samādhi became fully endowed with great learning,
and through that great learning has now realized unexcelled bodhi— I too should today likewise rejoice, even unto the desire to swiftly realize unexcelled bodhi."
"Bhadrapāla! This is the third mass of merit resulting from sympathetic joy of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"
That bodhisattva-mahāsattva should further reflect in this way:

"I have now learned by emulation that all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, when they originally practiced as bodhisattvas in the past, all attained this samādhi through sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); all became fully endowed with extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) because of this samādhi; and all attained Buddhahood by means of that extensive learning.

Now, by virtue of these merits of sympathetic joy, I vow to share them with all sentient beings, so that we may together give rise to sympathetic joy, together obtain this samādhi, together be endowed with extensive learning, and together fully accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Bhadrapāla! This is the fourth accumulation of merit resulting from sympathetic joy for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!"

Once that bodhisattva has achieved such sympathetic joy, such samādhi, such extensive learning, and such swift accomplishment of bodhi, they dedicate all these merits together with all sentient beings toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Such merits are difficult to measure; I shall now briefly reveal a small portion of them for you. You should listen attentively and reflect upon them well. "Bhadrapāla!
Suppose there were a person whose lifespan was fixed at one hundred years, whose body was light, whose breath was vigorous, and whose gait was as swift as flight.
As soon as this person was born, they would be able to travel through a single world-system;

first traveling eastward until reaching the very edge of that world-system, and likewise proceeding in succession to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below, circling through the ten directions until reaching the furthest limits of the earth.
Bhadrapāla! What do you think?

Suppose there were a person of extraordinary intelligence, well-versed in mathematics, who could calculate the distance—whether near or far, long or short—of the path traversed by this person across the realm of earth?
Bhadrapāla replied,
“No. [The Buddha asked,] “And can it be measured?”
"No. "Furthermore, can one observe it? "No."
“Can it also engage in reflection? “No,
World-Honored One.”
“Bhadrapāla! Let us set aside the beginner for a moment.

Suppose this person were to travel swiftly back and forth, reaching every one of the immeasurable worlds in the ten directions throughout a full hundred years; would that mathematician be able to know it?”
Bhadrapāla replied,
“No, World-Honored One!

If even those skilled in calculation cannot know the nearness or distance of the earth-element traversed during the first moment, how could they calculate the number of *yojanas* in the roadways of the countless worlds throughout the ten directions that such a person would traverse by flying with all their might for the duration of one lifetime?”
If one wishes to know it with certainty, only the World-Honored One, along with the great disciple Śāriputra and those non-regressive great bodhisattvas, are able to know it.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla: "So it is, so it is. I tell you now:

if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, having conceived a heart of faith and reverence, were to fill with precious jewels the worlds traversed by that Vāyu-caru person and offer them to the Buddhas of the ten directions, the merit they would obtain, though said to be extremely great, would still not equal even a small fraction of the merit of rejoicing in this samādhi."
Why is this? Bhadrapāla!

It is because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate this samādhi and, being fully endowed with the four kinds of sympathetic joy mentioned above, dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of seeking extensive learning and attaining perfect enlightenment.
Bhadrapāla!

For this reason, if one compares the merit of that gift with the virtue obtained from the preceding act of sympathetic joy, the former does not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousand-millionth part, or even a ten-billionth part; it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.

“Bhadrapāla! You should now know that the merit obtained by bodhisattvas through sympathetic joy and dedication is vast; therefore, I shall now further explain for you a small portion of the merit of a bodhisattva’s sympathetic joy. You should listen attentively.”
Bhadrapāla!

I recall that in the past, more than immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Siṃhamati Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Bhadrapāla!
At that time, within this world’s Jambudvīpa, the population was flourishing, with abundant wealth and treasures; it was prosperous, peaceful, and secure, and exceedingly delightful.
Bhadrapāla!
At that time, the land of this Jambudvīpa was vast and expansive, measuring eighteen thousand yojanas;
within it there were eighteen thousand cities and villages, all of which were composed of the seven precious jewels.
That city was twelve yojanas in length and breadth; within each of its various districts, there were nine hundred million households. "Bhadrapāla!
At that time, the great city was named Bhadramkara, and the residents therein numbered sixty billion. That city was the very place where the Tathāgata Siṃhamati was born."
Bhadrapāla!
At that time, during the first assembly when the Tathāgata Siṃhamati preached the Dharma, nine hundred million people realized the fruit of arhatship;
after seven days had passed, in the second assembly, another nine hundred million people attained the fruit of arhatship.
After the second assembly, in the third assembly there were another ninety billion people who attained the fruit of arhatship;

after the three assemblies had passed, another ninety billion people came from other directions for a great gathering—all of whom were pure bodhisattvas—and thereafter that Buddha constantly had immeasurable asaṃkhyeya assemblies of śrāvakas.

“Bhadrapāla! At that time, the people will practice the ten wholesome courses of action, just as those sentient beings in the future world of Maitreya Buddha will be fully accomplished in the ten types of karmic actions through his teaching.”
At that time, the human lifespan will be eighty-four thousand years, no different from the lifespan of humans during the time of Maitreya. "Bhadrapāla!

At that time, in that great city, there will be a universal monarch named Vijayavikrāmin who rules the world according to the Dharma. He will be endowed with the seven treasures—namely, the golden wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the military commander treasure; these are the seven treasures—and he will have a full thousand sons, whose physical forms are dignified and majestic, who possess heroic prowess, and who subdue all enemies."

The realm governed by that king extended to the very limits of the world; he did not employ weapons or military force, nor did he use intimidation, and there were no taxes or levies, for all necessities appeared spontaneously.
At that time, King Jayasena went to the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Siṃhamati, prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet, and then withdrew to sit to one side.

"At that time, the Tathāgata Siṃhamati, knowing that King Jayoṣadha’s heart was filled with longing and veneration, immediately proclaimed for him in detail the Samādhi of Manifest Presence (*pratyutpanna-samādhi*).
When the king had heard of this samādhi, he felt profound joy and, giving rise to a mind of sympathetic rejoicing, offered a handful of jewels, scattering them over the Buddha."

By virtue of this root of goodness from his sympathetic joy, after the king’s life ended, he was reborn in Jambudvīpa as a prince named Brahmadatta; he subsequently succeeded to the royal throne and ruled with righteousness.

After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, within the True Dharma there was a bhikṣu named Ratna, who was intelligent and diligent, and who constantly proclaimed and extensively expounded such sūtras for the fourfold assembly.

“Bhadrapāla! At that time, having heard of this samādhi from the bhikṣu, King Brahmadatta attained profound and pure faith and gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy; he then took a most excellent robe, worth hundreds of thousands, and covered the bhikṣu with it.”
Bhadrapāla!

Furthermore, after King Brahmadatta heard of this samādhi from the bhikṣu, he immediately resolved his mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; out of love for the Dharma, he abandoned his home to go forth, shaved off his hair and beard, and donned the kāṣāya robes.

At that time, there were also hundreds of thousands of people who had attained faith; they followed that king, donned the dharma robes, and left the household life for the sake of this very Samādhi Sūtra.

"At that time, the bhikṣu Brahmadatta, together with a multitude of one hundred thousand bhikṣus, served and made offerings to that Jewel Bhikṣu for eight thousand years without weariness; yet they were ultimately unable to attain such a samādhi, except for hearing it once."
Having heard this, they rejoice; they fully dedicate the merit of these four kinds of rejoicing toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, practicing extensively as they did with their initial rejoicing.

“Subsequently, the bhikṣu Brahmadatta and his assembly of hundreds of thousands, by virtue of these roots of goodness, soon encountered sixty-eight thousand Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; in every place where they were born, they always attained the status of being able to proclaim and extensively expound this samādhi for the sake of the multitudes.”

By virtue of those roots of goodness, that bhikṣu-king further encountered sixty-eight thousand *koṭis* of buddhas. In this manner, he successively planted various roots of goodness and attained this samādhi. Having fully perfected the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), he soon achieved *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, receiving the title Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān, named Dṛḍhavīrya (Firmly Diligent).

Furthermore, because those hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus attained this samādhi and were also able to accomplish the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), they have all already realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and are named Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas known as Dṛḍhavīra. They, in turn, cause immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

“Bhadrapāla! If even one who merely hears of it with their ears obtains such [benefits], how much more so for a bodhisattva who hears and accepts this samādhi, recites it, memorizes it, explains it extensively to others, and furthermore diligently contemplates and practices it—how could they fail to attain it?”
Bhadrapāla!
For this reason, among all bodhisattvas who hear of this samādhi, who would not rejoice in it?
Who would not recite and study it?
Who does not uphold it?
Who does not cultivate it?
Who does not expound it extensively?
Why is this? Bhadrapāla!
Because when those bodhisattvas hear this samādhi, they immediately achieve the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma) and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Bhadrapāla! For this reason, I now tell you: if there is a person who, with right faith and a pure mind, desires to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they must first, with a sincere heart, seek this samādhi.”
If a bodhisattva hears that within a distance of one hundred yojanas there exists this profound sūtra of samādhi, the bodhisattva should personally go there to listen to this scripture;
having heard it, they should immediately read, recite, receive and uphold, practice, contemplate, and extensively explain it to others.

“Bhadrapāla! Let alone going within a hundred yojanas to hear and receive it; furthermore, if that bodhisattva hears that this samādhi exists within two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, five hundred, or even a thousand yojanas in a certain city or village, the bodhisattva should personally go there to hear, recite, and uphold it.”
Why is this? Bhadrapāla!
It is because this bodhisattva possesses pure faith for the sake of seeking to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Therefore, a bodhisattva should not give rise to a mind of indolence, a mind of laziness, or a mind of distraction; rather, they should further arouse a mind of diligence and a mind of fierce intensity. For the sake of this samādhi, they should swiftly travel even a thousand yojanas, or at the very least, merely hear it—how much more so should they read, recite, receive and uphold it, contemplate it, and explain it?
Why is this? Bhadrapāla!
It is because this samādhi is able to encompass all factors conducive to enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
If there is a bodhisattva therein who, with a purely sincere mind, seeks to attain bodhi, they should travel as far as a thousand yojanas."

When listening to this samādhi dharma, a bodhisattva should serve and make offerings to that Dharma teacher, presenting all necessary requisites; they should constantly follow the Dharma teacher—whether for one year, two years, ten or twenty years, or even for a hundred years, or until the end of their life following the teacher without ever abandoning them—even if it is merely to seek to hear this samādhi, let alone being able to read, recite, receive and uphold it, contemplate its meaning, and explain it for others.

In this way, when a bodhisattva attends upon a Dharma teacher, they should set aside all their own personal concerns and always act in accordance with the intentions and conduct of that ācārya and Dharma teacher. They must serve them with a reverent mind and never disobey their instructions. They should give rise to a heart of respect and deep affection, abandoning all actions lacking love and reverence. Toward the Dharma teacher, they should conceive the thought of him as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), even to the point of regarding him as a Buddha.

“Bhadrapāla! Once that bodhisattva has given rise to such a heart of reverence and love toward that Dharma-master and ācārya, it shall never happen that they fail to read, recite, receive, uphold, contemplate, and extensively explain [this teaching], or even fail to hear this samādhi—unless, indeed, their karma from having previously slandered such profound sūtras has already ripened, such that they are certain to fall into the evil realms and their karma remains impure.”
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
Even if that bodhisattva should wish to depart from that Dharma teacher, he must always recognize the kindness, always remember the kindness, and always repay the kindness."
Why is this? Bhadrapāla!
It is because of the causes and conditions created by this Dharma-preacher’s proclamation that this sutra shall remain for a long time and not perish.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
