If a bodhisattva should even go a distance of a thousand yojanas for the sake of this samādhi, how much more so should they not fail to go to nearby cities, capitals, towns, villages, wildernesses, or mountains and forests to listen to it, receive it, recite it, contemplate its meaning, and explain it extensively to others?"
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla! I tell you now:

if there is a bodhisattva who, for the sake of this samādhi, travels as far as a thousand yojanas only to find that he cannot hear it, even though that bodhisattva does not hear this samādhi, he should nevertheless seek roots of goodness within this Dharma, rouse his vigor, and never succumb to indolence."

You should know that such a person has already attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; how much more so for one who hears it, receives and upholds it, recites it, contemplates and practices it, and extensively proclaims it to others?

“Bhadrapāla! You should now observe that those bodhisattvas who, having heard this samādhi, are able to receive, uphold, contemplate, and practice it, immediately attain such a vast accumulation of merit;
even those who, though seeking it, cannot hear it, shall likewise be fully endowed with many great roots of goodness.”

If those who merely hear it—even if they do not themselves hear it—are all already established on the stage of non-retrogression and will ultimately achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how much more so for those who, having heard it, read and recite it, receive and uphold it, contemplate and practice it, and extensively explain it to others, and furthermore cause many others to hear it and likewise recite, uphold, practice, contemplate, and zealously propagate it?
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"I recall that in the past there was a Tathāgata, Named Siṃhamati, the Supreme among Men.
At that time, there was a king who was the leader of the multitude; He went in person to the Buddha to seek this samādhi."
When King Mahāprajña heard this, his joy was so pervasive that it could not be described;
holding precious jewels in his hands, he scattered them as an offering to the Honored One among Men, Siṃhamati.
Reflecting within his mind, he uttered these words:
"I now take refuge in the Unsurpassed Awakening, which brings benefit to all the worlds; I pray only that you will skillfully explain samādhi."
When the king had completed this undertaking, he relinquished his body and was reborn in that very palace;
there he soon encountered the Bhikṣu Ratna, a man of great virtue whose fame filled the ten directions.
When he heard the bhikṣu’s excellent discourse, his heart was filled with immeasurable joy;
he immediately offered robes of exquisite jewels as a response to that bhikṣu for the sake of awakening.
Furthermore, he went forth from the household life together with several thousand followers,
serving and making offerings to that bhikṣu for a full eight thousand years, all for the sake of seeking this samādhi.
He taught this once and did not proclaim it again; hearing and receiving this profound and wondrous [teaching] was like the great ocean.
At that time, his mind and intellect were entirely without weariness as he sought this truly real, supreme, and tranquil dhyāna.
Having practiced in this manner, they encountered sixty thousand and eight thousand Buddhas, great and majestic heroes, and during that time they also heard this samādhi.
In other lifetimes, he again made offerings and served sixty-eight thousand billion World-Honored Ones;
all that he heard of the profound and wondrous teachings he rejoiced in, all because of the Tathāgata Siṃha.
That king, having thus practiced with such diligence, At last attained Buddhahood under the name Dṛḍhavīrya;
He transformed immeasurable numbers of sentient beings, Causing them to distance themselves from the dust of birth and death wherever they were.
Thousands of followers who left the household life with the king Also likewise attained Buddhahood, named Dṛḍhasūra.
The sound of their virtue fills the ten directions; hearing the name of this samādhi, they realize great awakening.
How much more so for those who can explain it to others, remaining unstained by attachment to any world?
One should further extensively manifest sublime reflection, as the Buddhas have expounded this samādhi.
If one knows that this samādhi exists a hundred yojanas away, one should travel there to hear it for the sake of seeking bodhi;
do not weary yourself with the verbal instructions, for the merit of those who hear it is immeasurable.
If one were to reach that place but fail to hear it, one would still obtain a multitude of various merits;
how much more so for those who, having heard it, contemplate and explain it?
One should only swiftly seek this samādhi.
One should keep in mind that person endowed with pure virtues; approach and serve them without weariness.
Whichever bhikṣu possesses this sūtra, one should go to him and practice offerings.

16. Chapter on Awakening. The *Bhadrapāla-parivarta* of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, Chapter Sixteen: The Chapter on Awakening. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying: "Bhadrapāla!"
I recall that in the past, more than immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Saccanāma Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Varuṇa who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, extensively proclaimed and expounded this Samādhi Sūtra.
At that time, I was a great king who single-mindedly sought this wondrous samādhi; then, within a dream, I heard a voice announcing the location of this samādhi.

Having awakened, he then went in person to the place of his bhikṣu teacher to seek this samādhi; he subsequently requested the Dharma Master to shave his hair and allow him to leave the household life for the sake of seeking to hear and receive this samādhi.
"I personally served the Dharma Master Samantacakra for a full thirty-six thousand years, yet because the celestial Māras obstructed me, I ultimately did not hear it.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, saying:
"I now tell you: you should all listen to and receive this King of Samādhis with urgency; do not be dilatory, nor forget it. Serve your teacher well, so as not to lose its essence."

Regarding this samādhi of seeking, one should take its attainment as the goal; even if it takes an eon or up to hundreds of thousands of eons, one should not give rise to a mind of indolence, and there is nothing that cannot be attained.
"Bhadrapāla!..."

If a person seeks this samādhi with single-minded devotion, they should never leave their teacher but always follow them, providing offerings—namely, medicinal decoctions, food and drink, clothing, bedding, various requisites, and all manner of gold, silver, and precious gems. Whatever resources are needed should be offered to the teacher without any sense of stinginess; even if one lacks these oneself, one should beg for them to give. One should strive to attain this samādhi and never give rise to a mind of weariness.
“Bhadrapāla! Let us set aside such ordinary offerings for a moment.
One who seeks the Dharma, if the teacher has need of anything—even to the point of cutting their own body, skin, or limbs—should offer them to the teacher.”
"If the Master were to require my life, I would not begrudge it; how much less would I fail to offer other external things to him?
O Bhadrapāla! Such is the manner in which one who seeks the Dharma serves, protects, and accords with a Dharma teacher."
Furthermore, serving one's teacher should be like a slave following his master or a minister serving his sovereign; serving the teacher is likewise so.

Such a person will swiftly attain samādhi. Having attained samādhi, they should maintain mindfulness and uphold it, constantly remembering the teacher's kindness and always contemplating how to repay it.

"Bhadrapāla! This jewel of a samādhi is not easily heard. Even if someone were to spend more than a hundred thousand kalpas seeking merely to hear its name, they would still not hear it; how much less so could they hear it, write it down, recite and uphold it, and furthermore explain it in detail for others?"

“Bhadrapāla! Suppose one were to fill as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges with precious jewels and practice dāna by offering them; although such merit would be vast, it would still not equal the incalculable merit obtained from hearing the name of this sutra or writing down a single verse.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:

"I recall in the past, immeasurable eons ago, For a full six thousand years, I constantly followed a Dharma Master without ever leaving him for a moment; Yet, at first, I did not hear the name of this samādhi."
There was a Buddha whose name was Zhicheng (Supreme Sincerity); at that time, there was a bhikṣu named Huelun.
After the World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu extensively expounded this samādhi.
At that time, I was the king of that realm, and in a dream I heard an announcement regarding the place of samādhi:
"The bhikṣu Varuṇa constantly proclaims and turns [the wheel]; Your Majesty should listen to and receive this wondrous sūtra."
Having awakened from the dream, he immediately sought it out;
he went in person to the bhikṣu to request the samādhi, whereupon he relinquished his royal throne and left the household life, reverently making offerings without ceasing for even a moment.
Having passed thirty-six thousand years, I have only wished to encounter its proclamation;
yet, constantly disturbed by the arrival of celestial Māras, I have ultimately failed to hear it even once.
Therefore, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen,
I exhort you with these sincere words:
you should strive to uphold this samādhi.
If one wishes to reverently serve that Dharma Master for the duration of one kalpa or many kalpas,
providing medicinal decoctions and various exquisite foods in order to seek out and hear such a Samādhi Sūtra;
and furthermore, prepares billions of garments, bedding, lamps, candles, and various treasures—
Exerting themselves with such diligence, they feel no weariness, for the sake of hearing this wondrous samādhi.
A bhikṣu should personally beg and offer it; he would not begrudge even his own body and life, let alone have any thought of attachment toward other things.
One who seeks in this manner attains samādhi;
receiving grace, they constantly bear it in mind and contemplate repaying that kindness. When a wise person has heard this, they should explain it extensively;
having sought with single-minded diligence for billions of nayutas of kalpas, one finally hears this wondrous samādhi.
Even if one were to fill as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges with precious jewels and practice *dāna*,
the merit of one who can recite a single verse therein would surpass that of the former.
One who correctly proclaims even a single verse surpasses [the merit of] nayutas of kalpas;
how much more so for one who, having heard it, can propagate it widely?
The merit of such a person is unspeakable.
If a person delights in practicing for enlightenment, they should seek this Dharma for the sake of all beings;
they will surely attain the realization of the unsurpassed path and, having heard it, abide securely within this samādhi.

Chapter 17: Entrustment. The Great Collection Sūtra, Section on Bhadrapāla, Chapter Seventeen: Entrustment. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying: "Bhadrapāla!"
Therefore, those sons of good family who possess pure faith should always apply themselves with diligence to hearing this samādhi;

having heard and received it, they should read and recite it, maintain it in memory, contemplate its meaning, extensively explain and expound it for the sake of the world, and skillfully transcribe it to place it within a treasury.
Why is this so? Bhadrapāla!
In the future world after my parinirvāṇa, there will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of pure faith who, for the sake of sentient beings, shall seek extensive learning.
In order to seek extensive learning, one should travel to various regions to hear and receive the True Dharma.
O Bhadrapāla!

Therefore, those sons of good family who possess a longing for it, who are endowed with faith, who uphold the True Dharma, who love and delight in the True Dharma, and who maintain the sūtras—for the sake of widely proclaiming [the teaching] to such as these, and through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s power—should transcribe such Mahāyāna sūtras, seal them with the seal of the Tathāgata, and thereafter place them within a casket for safekeeping.
“Bhadrapāla! In this regard, what is the seal of the Tathāgata?
It is that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are without creation and without action.”
There is no creator; it has never existed as unconditioned, signless, thoughtless, independent, ungraspable, non-appropriative, and non-abiding.
All conditioned formations are exhausted; the cause of suffering is exhausted;
existence is exhausted, and all afflictions are exhausted.

There is neither arising nor ceasing; there is neither the path nor the fruit of the path. All noble ones have nothing to conceal; it is reviled by the ignorant, praised by the wise, and accepted by those who are skillful.
When the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, spoke this sutra, immeasurable sentient beings all planted various roots of goodness for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

In those Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there are immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* assemblies of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have all come here from their own lands; they have all come for the purpose of hearing and receiving this samādhi, and they have all attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the entire great earth of this trichiliocosm shook in six ways—namely, it moved, shook greatly, and shook all over; it surged, surged greatly, and surged all over; it rose, rose greatly, and rose all over; it quaked, quaked greatly, and quaked all over; it roared, roared greatly, and roared all over; it trembled, trembled greatly, and trembled all over—even to the point where the periphery surged while the center subsided, and the center surged while the periphery subsided—and thus did this world shake so violently.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, and the Venerable Ānanda, as well as the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, Ratnaśrī the Licchavi, the Elder Sārthavāha, the Elder’s Son Tārakṣa, the Young Brahmin Mahāśrī, the Elder Varuṇadeva, and the assembly of five hundred followers, along with the other devas, worldlings, and the fourfold assembly, saying: “Kāśyapa!

I now entrust to you this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which I have cultivated and perfected over three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas; such meanings as these cannot be believed by anyone in the entire world.

Why is this? Because the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata are most supreme and subtle, foremost and profound; in future ages, they will be able to bestow upon all sentient beings anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Therefore, I now earnestly entrust this to you: you should listen to it and receive it; you should read and recite it; you should remember and uphold it; you should contemplate it; you should practice it; you should bring it forth; you should proclaim it widely; you should explain it; you should perfect it; and you should disseminate it so that it shall not be interrupted.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to practice this Samādhi Sūtra, who wish to read and recite it, who wish to receive and uphold it, who wish to contemplate it, who wish to reveal it, or who wish to explain it extensively, they should cause others to give rise to right faith, cause them to read and recite it, cause them to receive and uphold it, cause them to contemplate it, cause them to reveal it, and cause them to explain it extensively."

Having now extensively expounded this for those sons and daughters of good family who dwell securely in the Mahāyāna, you should train yourselves accordingly and always keep this instruction of mine in mind.

When the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Ānanda, and all the other great śrāvakas; as well as the assembly of five hundred upāsakas, including Bhadrapāla, Ratnākara, Susārthavāha, Jyotipāla, Mahāpāla, and Varuṇa the Elder; and the multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had come from the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; and even all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans—hearing what the Tathāgata had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced and practiced in accordance with his teachings.
